articles.title: Scans for Sshole Vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158), (Sun, Nov 8th)
articles.context: With the emergence of the "sshole" vulnerability last week, we are now seeing an increase in attempts to exploit the vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Our honeypots use "Cowrie" to collect SSH data. With the emergence of the "sshole" vulnerability last week, we are now seeing an increase in attempts to exploit the vulnerability. Our data is a bit limited in this respect. Our honeypots collect only the first 255 characters of SSH passwords. Longer passwords are highly unusual and not used for the usual password brute-forcing we observe.

Our data starts showing the increase of the use of long passwords on November 1st. Since then, the number of requests has been increasing:

A typical "buggy" password is:

articles.title: Attackers Exploit Third-Party Provider to Raid French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa
articles.context: French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says hackers exploited a service provider to steal up to $133 million using the bank’s own account
articles.full_text:
French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says hackers exploited a service provider to steal up to $133 million using the bank’s own account.

French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was hit by a cyberattack that let attackers make fraudulent transactions of up to $133 million, forcing it to suspend certain systems. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa is a major French cooperative banking and insurance group headquartered in Brest, Brittany, France.

The bank says the attacker used its own account to send transactions to other banking organizations, and that customer assets weren’t affected.

“French lender Credit Mutuel Arkea said on Thursday hackers had stolen around €100 million ($112.61 million) in a cyber heist and it was working to try to recover the money, in a rare case of cybercriminals successfully stealing from a mainstream bank.” Reuters states.

Blockchain researcher ZachXBT first warned of a large unauthorized withdrawal from multiple centralized exchange accounts a day earlier. He said the attacker may have stolen up to 118 million euros ($133 million) and withdrawn it as the USDC and USDT stablecoins.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains.” ZachXBT wrote.

“While the illicit actor remains unidentified, I can say with a high degree of confidence it is NOT Lazarus Group based on multiple laundering indicators.”

The attacker remains unidentified, but ZachXBT believes it is highly unlikely to be Lazarus Group, based on money-laundering patterns.

According to BleepingComputer, the expert pointed out that the lack of public disclosure allowed attackers to launder $30 million by November 3, potentially preventing EU authorities from freezing the funds. The Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime unit opened an investigation after receiving a complaint from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, with France’s cybercrime police leading the probe.

Arkéa disclosed the incident on November 4, saying it was contained, customer assets were unaffected and some transfers had been delayed. Attackers reportedly accessed the bank through a service provider’s platform, not Fortuneo, and used Arkéa’s own account to move funds through other banks and convert them into cryptocurrency. The bank also warned customers about increased phishing risks.

“Crédit Mutuel Arkéa announces that it has been the target of an attack that enabled the execution of fraudulent transactions.” reads the notice published by the bank. “Upon detecting this attack, and in accordance with standard procedures, the Group contacted the relevant regulatory and supervisory authorities to inform them of the situation.” “This incident is now closed and fully under control. Operations are gradually resuming this morning, following thorough verification by the Group and its subsidiaries and the implementation of enhanced security measures.”

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says customer assets were unaffected, although some transfers were delayed. The bank maintains its financial stability, warns of possible phishing attempts and urges customers not to share sensitive information. Its teams are assessing the incident and strengthening security measures, with further updates expected.

Arkéa did not confirm ZachXBT’s reported figure but acknowledged significant losses and said some funds were blocked. The bank ruled out internal human error, described the incident as a sophisticated attack and is working with law enforcement to identify the attackers and establish how the breach occurred.

When the FAQ asked whether 118 million euros had been stolen, Arkéa wouldn’t give a number: We do not confirm this information and can only validate the order of magnitude.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa)

articles.title: Week in review: Refrigeration cyberattacks hit European retailers again, Patch Tuesday forecast
articles.context: Patched Zyxel GS1900 switches remained open to in-the-wild exploit (CVE-2026-107441) Zyxel GS1900 series network switches that received a fix for a flaw that was later reported...
articles.full_text:
Here’s an overview of some of last week’s most interesting news, articles, interviews and videos:

The first ten lines of a command policy for AI coding agents In this Help Net Security interview, Vinay Thakker, CTO of KloudStax, explains how to set identity, credentials, and network limits for AI agents. He argues that agents should run under their own identity, with the person’s identity attached when acting on someone’s behalf.

Google disrupts XCPE botnet, bans the company behind it Google shut down the servers behind XCPE, a backdoor hidden in the firmware of Android TV set-top boxes. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group attributes the operation with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, the company that manufactured many of those boxes. More than 1.3 million devices were enrolled.

Fireperf: Open-source network testing tool for firewalls and routers The IPFire project has released fireperf, an open-source measurement tool that opens connections at a fixed rate and reports what the device in the middle did with each one. It is free software aimed at administrators, developers and testers who evaluate firewalls, routers and other systems that keep a state for every connection.

AI coding agents are installing MCP servers that will never be patched When a developer tells an AI coding agent to “set up a GitHub MCP,” the agent has to pick a package. New research from Glow Labs documents sessions where it picked one out of an archived repository that will never be patched again.

What human hackers still do better than AI, according to HackerOne’s CEO AI can find vulnerabilities in minutes, but people still hold the edge in judging what a flaw means for a business. In this Help Net Security interview, Kara Sprague, CEO of HackerOne, talks about business logic bugs, what AI does to the crowd model, and why routine medium-severity findings may pay less.

What AI-generated malware looks like under the microscope In this Help Net Security interview, Lindsay Kaye, VP of Threat Intelligence at HUMAN Security, talks about what AI-generated malware looks like on the bench. She points to tidy comments, uniform logging messages, and emojis as signs a script came from a model, and notes that decompiled code strips much of that away.

AI agent detection signals that still work when agents look human Bots follow a script. AI agents work toward a goal and choose their own steps, which makes them harder to catch. In this Help Net Security interview, Zohaib Ahmed, CEO of Resemble AI explains how agents arrive as declared, undeclared or disguised traffic, and why binary bot detection misses the last two groups.

A banking malware sample led researchers to an Android bug that can loop-crash phones Bitdefender Labs researchers built an Android app that contains no executable code and requests no permissions, and installing it leaves a Pixel 10 in a crash loop that can take a factory reset to clear. The flaw, which Bitdefender calls GhostMap, comes from how Android reads the ZIP structure inside an APK.

Security certification is a snapshot, and buyers read too much into it In this Help Net Security video, Mariia Bakhtina, a research specialist at Masaryk University, explains what a Common Criteria or FIPS-140 certificate does and does not promise. In her team’s analysis, about 6 in 10 vulnerabilities matched to certified products, smartcards aside, were disclosed after the certification date.

Chainalysis breached using “offensive agentic techniques” Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis has suffered a cybersecurity incident that led to a data breach. According to the company’s Friday announcement, the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance hack.

Second wave of refrigeration cyberattacks hits European supermarkets Three weeks after the attack that turned refrigeration units in French supermarkets into ovens overnight, similar cyberattacks have hit shops in other European countries and again caused refrigerated food to be spoiled.

CISA to federal agencies: Remediate exploited Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527) CISA added two new Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday, after Ivanti updated an earlier security advisory with details about the flaws.

AI agents scale and speed up Chinese-linked attacks A China-nexus espionage group used AI agents to attack more than 200 organizations in 11 days, CrowdStrike said last week. On Monday, Kaspersky published details of a separate campaign against educational institutions in Africa and Latin America, mounted by Chinese-speaking operators.

Poisoned cPGuard update hits thousands of web hosting servers An attacker has compromised the update infrastructure of cPGuard, a security suite for Linux web hosting servers, and pushed out a malicious update to nearly 3,000 customer servers. OPSShield, the company behind the security suite, also confirmed that the attacker made off with customer contact information and hashed passwords from the firm’s billing and licensing server.

Cyberattack hits French blood banks Three blood banks have detected and reversed a potentially destructive temperature spike in their cold rooms, following a cyberattack that targeted a refrigeration equipment provider of the French Blood Establishment (EFS), the only civilian blood collection and transfusion organization in France.

Patched Zyxel GS1900 switches remained open to in-the-wild exploit (CVE-2026-107441) Zyxel GS1900 series network switches that received a fix for a flaw that was later reported to have been exploited in the wild are still open to an exploit attackers used, Binarly found. That’s because the patch fixed a different bug (CVE-2026-7273) from the one (CVE-2026-107441) the exploit actually relies on.

Vercel ties login sessions to devices, rolls out AI security reviews in public beta Vercel, the popular cloud platform for building and hosting websites and web applications, has announced the rollout of Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) and the launch of Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Product showcase: Sweet Virtual Patching stops HTTP2Shell while fixes catch up Sweet Security helps teams identify exposed services at runtime, and its Virtual Patching blocks the system call the demonstrated exploit uses to launch a shell, buying time to deploy permanent fixes.

Opal’s agent.ID virtual event: Top security leaders on governing Al agents Opal Security hosted agent.ID, a free virtual event focused on adapting identity and access management (IAM) to AI agents, on November 5, 2026. The event brought together CISOs and identity leaders from Elastic, Instacart, Notion, Databricks, Knostic and other organizations to discuss how agents could be governed through assigned ownership, defined permissions and accountability.

Novee puts forgotten internet-facing assets through penetration testing Novee’s External Surface Testing is a new capability in its AI penetration testing platform that helps security teams discover internet-facing assets and validate exploitable vulnerabilities. It tests newly disclosed CVEs and findings imported from third-party external attack surface management (EASM) tools.

Secure your containers without breaking what works Container security has a familiar problem. Teams identify vulnerabilities, but turning those findings into lower risk is much harder. A standard container image may include operating-system packages, development tools, debugging utilities and libraries that an application never uses. Each unnecessary component can expand the attack surface and add vulnerabilities to investigate, patch or explain during an audit.

Live Q&A: CISSP exam prep with ISC2 experts ISC2 hosted a live Q&A about the CISSP exam on November 6, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. CET. Experts answered questions, explained certification requirements, reviewed the exam domains, and shared self-study resources and training options.

November 2026 Patch Tuesday forecast: Old software continues to bite Still working through October’s Patch Tuesday updates, or ready for another round next week? Microsoft fixed a record-breaking 1,400-plus vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-96951, an actively exploited Windows Shell flaw that bypasses Mark of the Web protections. October also brought PHP2Shell: two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on web servers. Emergency patches are available.

Ransomware gang talked AI agents into doing much of its dirty work The group behind the Aur0ra ransomware has been using AI agents to move through victim networks, collect credentials and work its way up to domain administrator access, according to Sophos.

FBI pins $6.3 billion Binance crypto heist on North Korea while scammers circle anxious users North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the FBI has confirmed. The agency tied the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean group it named in the $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis were the first to attribute the heist to the group, within a day of the attack.

AI-powered infostealer picks out the most profitable parts of your stolen data A new Windows infostealer sends the data it steals to an AI model and asks it to rank the victim’s assets by how much money they could bring in, Cisco Talos has found.

Stolen AI access leaves companies with cloud bills of up to $1 million Criminals who break into corporate cloud accounts are using the stolen access to run AI models at the victim’s expense, in some cases racking up more than $100,000 in charges in a single day, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant researchers have found.

Attackers exploit critical Node-RED flaw to deploy Linux bot and backdoors (CVE-2026-58115) Attackers are exploiting an authentication flaw (CVE-2026-58115) in Node-RED, a programming tool built into some industrial control products, to install a Linux bot and backdoors on unprotected servers, VulnCheck has found.

Police seize over 100 servers linked to investment fraud with more than €4 million in losses Seven people have been arrested and more than 100 servers seized in a coordinated law enforcement action against an investment fraud network that started unravelling after a complaint from a German couple.

Fake job interview opened the door to $6.34 billion Binance heist A tampered software installer and a fake job interview gave attackers the access they needed to steal about $6.34 billion in digital assets from Binance. The money left Binance wallets on October 29, in what is likely the biggest crypto heist in the history. Tether, Circle and other partners helped freeze close to $3 billion of the stolen funds within the first day, and the exchange promised to cover all user losses.

Russian hackers target iOS and Android users with n-day exploits Russia’s APT29 has been using compromised websites, lookalike domains and a hijacked web analytics service to target iOS and Android users with exploits for patched flaws and steal their cookies, messages and Wi-Fi passwords, according to Sekoia.

OpenAI’s upcoming AI model built 948 working Linux root exploits in a single run An automated system running on an upcoming AI model turned hundreds of Linux kernel bugs into working exploits that give an ordinary user root access, and wrote a patch for each underlying flaw, OpenAI revealed in a new research post.

Scammers capitalize on GTA 6 hype to push malware and crypto cons Scammers are offering supposed leaked builds, early copies and phone versions of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) weeks before the game’s November 19 launch, Netcraft warned in a new blog post.

Cyberattack on Norway’s aid agency may have swept up all user data The names and email addresses of 20,614 people registered on Norad’s Grants Portal may have ended up in the hands of attackers, Norway’s development aid agency has disclosed.

Rental phishing sites use live chat to win over hesitant travelers Holiday travelers looking for a place to stay are landing on copies of popular rental platforms, complete with host names, ratings and reviews, that ask for their passwords, personal details and credit card numbers. The sites, spotted and taken down by Fortra’s Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team, rely on familiar branding, copied property listings and reservation details, along with urgent messages meant to rush visitors into acting.

Residential proxy traffic caught leaving the White House network The White House network has been working as an exit point for residential proxy services, a setup that may open a path into one of the most closely guarded networks in the world, Layer3 Intel found.

OpenSSH flaw exploited in the wild just hours after disclosure (CVE-2026-123158) An OpenSSH flaw that lets remote attackers log into passwordless accounts on Alpine Linux and other musl-based systems is being exploited, threat intelligence firm Previdian has warned.

US agencies warn attackers are targeting refrigeration systems that protect food and medicine Threat actors are going after the controllers that keep grocery store freezers and cold storage rooms at safe temperatures, and they may push those units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, five US federal agencies warned in a joint advisory published on Thursday.

Product showcase: Trust Onion uses rotating codewords to verify callers Trust Onion is a free app that gives trusted groups three rotating codewords to check who they are communicating with. It also includes signed selfies, message checks, and callback requests. It is available for macOS, iOS, and Android.

Byoky: Open-source wallet for AI API keys Byoky is an open-source wallet for AI API keys, available as a Chrome and Firefox extension and as iOS and Android apps. Users store their keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and other providers in it, encrypted on their own device.

DeepSeek open-sources Super-Agent, a coding agent that watches team chats for work Deepseek released a research prototype of dsh-superagent, a coding agent that does work on a GitHub repository for you. The agent gets to work in two situations: an allowed user asks for something, or a rule your team wrote covers it. You can also open up a chat or GitHub scope, and then anyone in it can request work just by mentioning the agent.

OpenAI raises top bug bounty payout to $172,000 with bonuses OpenAI increased its security bug bounties to encourage independent researchers to find vulnerabilities in its software. The program now offers bonuses for high-quality reports.

Gorbag APT group hits Ukrainian courts and city councils with self-deleting malware ESET has been tracking a Russia-aligned group it calls Gorbag, which has been breaking into Ukrainian organizations since at least February 2025 using spearphishing attachments and a stealer that erases itself once the data is gone.

Anthropic open-sources FlashProve, its provable inference prototype for MoE models Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team, with collaborators at EPFL, MIT and StarkWare, built FlashProve, a prototype that produces a cryptographic proof that one specific language model generated one specific reply. The prover, two verifiers, the formal proofs behind them and a protocol specification are on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license.

NIST publishes cybersecurity guide for businesses too small to have IT staff The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released cybersecurity guidance for small businesses with no paid employees other than their owners. These businesses include freelancers, sole proprietors, and independent contractors.

Companies going all in on AI could see their strategy backfire Four of the five highest-ranked enterprise risks in Gartner’s Quarterly Emerging Risk Report were AI-related. AI strategy miscalculation and AI-driven competitive displacement debuted at No. 3 and No. 4, respectively. The AI workforce preparedness gap held fifth place.

Ghostunnel: Open-source TLS proxy with mutual authentication Ghostunnel is an open-source proxy that handles TLS for programs that cannot handle it themselves. It works in two directions. In server mode it sits in front of a backend, accepts TLS connections, checks the client’s certificate, then passes traffic to the service behind it over TCP or a UNIX socket. In client mode it does the reverse, listening for plain local connections, wrapping them in TLS and presenting a client certificate to the remote service.

Open-source file sync tool rsync 3.5.2 fixes a CPU exhaustion flaw The rsync project released version 3.5.2, and it closes a flaw that let a connecting client tie up a server’s CPU with checksum math that leads nowhere. The new version also lets you push a transfer to the back of the queue for CPU and disk, so a big sync stops elbowing everything else on the machine.

Most consumers aren’t ready to let AI agents shop unsupervised Customer control, account security and ease of use are influencing the adoption of AI agents that make purchases, book services and access personal information, according to Okta’s 2026 Customer Identity Trends Report.

Companies are spending more on AI governance and getting less control Companies are increasing their cybersecurity budgets, with AI security and governance the top priority for additional spending, followed by cloud security, according to DNSFilter’s The Cost of Shadow AI report.

Healthcare can’t govern the AI tools it hasn’t found yet Nearly nine in ten healthcare leaders say security or compliance staff always or usually review AI-written code that touches patient data before it goes live, and seven in ten have still found an AI-built tool handling that data without IT or security knowing, according to Paubox.

Apple is bringing harmful content checks to iCloud link sharing with potential account penalties Apple will begin checking iCloud content shared using the “Anyone with the link” option for harmful material in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.3 or later. When sharing content stored in iCloud, users can choose “Share a Link” or “Send a Copy.” Those who choose “Share a Link” can restrict access to people they invite or approve, or allow anyone with the link to access the content.

Google puts new limits on AI agents that hunt threats and fix vulnerabilities Google Cloud is adding new controls to CodeMender, its AI tool for finding and fixing software vulnerabilities, allowing businesses to isolate attack simulations and target code scans more precisely.

99% of repository access tokens never expire Developers, automated tools and AI coding agents hold permissions that can outlast the work they were granted for. Without access reviews, organizations can leave accounts able to copy or change company code after the work ends, according to BlueFlag Security’s The State of Developer Risk 2026 report.

87% say their AI controls need to work better The AI running inside large companies has stopped waiting for permission. Across five categories of AI, from chatbots to process automation, more than half of 3,600 business decision-makers say the systems their teams use can act within defined rules without routine review, or finish whole processes with no human approval.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber found 81 Firefox flaws earlier AI testing missed OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a version of GPT-6 Astra trained to find software vulnerabilities, test how attackers could exploit them, and help develop fixes. The model is designed for authorized security testing of websites and applications.

Cybersecurity jobs available right now: November 3, 2026 We’ve scoured the market to bring you a selection of roles that span various skill levels within the cybersecurity field. Check out this weekly selection of cybersecurity jobs available right now.

articles.title: CTM360 Exposes Fake Gift Card Scams Exploiting Trusted Brands
articles.context: Threat actors exploit consumer familiarity with established brands, frequently impersonating major retailers and consumer platforms such as PlayStation, Sephora, SHEIN, Walmart,...
articles.full_text:
Fraudulent reward portals and fake gift card giveaways are surging globally, tricking users into deceptive verification loops and paid subscriptions.

These scams lure victims with a simple pitch: click an ad featuring a celebrity endorsement, claim a free gift card from a well-known brand, and complete a quick "human verification" step to unlock the reward.

Read the full report here: https://www.ctm360.com/reports/gift-card-scams

Behind the polished branding, fake progress bars, and convincing promotional messages, however, no actual gift cards are provided.

Instead, these campaigns operate as large-scale affiliate monetization schemes designed to collect personal information, generate application installs, and enroll unsuspecting users in recurring mobile subscriptions.

1,000+ Incidents Exploiting Trusted Brands

Based on activity observed by CTM360, analysts identified more than 1,000 incidents linked to this recurring campaign.

Threat actors exploit consumer familiarity with established brands, frequently impersonating major retailers and consumer platforms such as PlayStation, Sephora, SHEIN, Walmart, and Amazon.

To increase credibility and attract potential victims, the campaigns rely heavily on social media distribution through:

Sponsored social media ads

Viral posts promoting "giveaways"

Fabricated endorsements from high-profile celebrities and influencers (such as MrBeast or Alix Earle)

Because the underlying infrastructure is highly modular, threat actors can swap out the impersonated brand, celebrity lure, and domain name without rebuilding the core scam engine.

How the Campaign Works: The Fake Generation Trap

CTM360 maps this activity using a structured fraud lifecycle, highlighting how victims are systematically pushed through a psychological progression of curiosity, trust, and urgency.

Once a user clicks a malicious ad, they are redirected to a fraudulent reward portal.

To appear credible, these websites display:

Cloned brand logos and colors

Fake participant numbers and live countdown timers

Fabricated testimonials from "recent winners"

After a victim selects a gift card value, the site runs a scripted, visual progress animation simulating the generation of the card on the back end.

The portal then displays a partially masked code (e.g., XXXX-XXXX-7F3A-XXXX) to convince the user that the reward is real and ready to claim.

Before the full code is revealed, the victim is presented with a deceptive "Security Check" or "Human Verification" gate.

Download The Gift Card Scam Report

Discover how threat actors use brand impersonation and fake rewards to exploit users.

Get insights into attacker infrastructure and learn to defend your organization with CTM360's Digital Risk Protection.

Download Now

The Endless Verification Loop and Monetization

The "human verification" step is a deceptive pivot into what CTM360 identifies as "Trap 10." Rather than performing a legitimate security check, the verification process redirects victims to third-party activities designed to generate revenue for the operators.

Victims are pushed into an endless loop of:

Completing surveys, quizzes, and promotional offers.

Installing unwanted third-party applications or browser extensions.

Subscribing to paid mobile services through localized carrier-billing mechanisms

If a user completes a task, they are not given the gift card. The site simply reports the step as "incomplete" and pushes the victim to another offer. In all flows tested by CTM360, no reward was ever delivered.

Technical Observations: Affiliate Hand-Offs

Unlike traditional phishing that steals user credentials, this campaign operates on a volume-and-conversion model.

CTM360 observed that lure pages redirect victims through affiliate tracking URLs (e.g., passing parameters like offer_id and aff_id). This tracking token links the victim's registration directly to the threat actor's affiliate network account.

When a victim completes a mobile number submission and PIN/OTP verification for a subscription, the threat actor earns a commission.

Risks to Users and Organizations

For the victim, the fallout goes beyond wasted time. Consequences include personal information exposure, unexpected mobile billing charges, and an influx of spam.

For organizations, this represents a severe abuse of brand reputation. The campaign highlights a broader trend: attackers are operating at scale, weaponizing brand trust as a mechanism to drive lucrative affiliate conversions.

articles.title: SonicWall Patches Exploited SonicOS Vulnerability That Weakens VPN Logins
articles.context: SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks
articles.full_text:
SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw affects the SSL VPN component of SonicOS, the operating system that runs on SonicWall firewalls. It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6.

“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA),” reads SonicWall’s description of CVE-2026-19868.

According to the vendor, an SSL VPN is exposed only if SAML-based login is enabled. CVE-2026-19868 has a CVSS score of 7.1, which puts it in the high-severity range. The flaw was reported by Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office.

SonicWall said its product security team “has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability.”

CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Neither the vendor nor CISA has shared any details about the suspected attacks. It’s also unclear whether the flaw was exploited as a zero-day, before a patch became available.

Impacted devices include Gen7 TZ, NSa, NSsp and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or older. Gen8 TZ, NSa and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 8.2.2-8015 or older are also affected.

SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.

SonicWall’s advisory doesn’t mark any of the other six flaws as exploited. Two of them, each with a CVSS score of 8.8, affect the SonicOS management interface. One is a permissive cross-domain policy issue and the other is a session validation bug.

Under certain circumstances, a remote attacker could abuse either one without logging in to take unauthorized actions.

Three of the remaining flaws are pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL VPN service and the TACACS+ authentication client. Attackers could use them to launch DoS attacks at the application level.

The last one is a weak password hashing issue in virtual appliances. An attacker who already has high-privileged local access could exploit it to obtain a platform credential, which gives access to some of the platform’s settings.

Threat actors often exploit SonicWall product vulnerabilities. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 20 security holes, but the agency has yet to add CVE-2026-102255, which hackers started targeting last month, just days after its disclosure.

articles.title: SonicWall warns of new SSL-VPN MFA bypass flaw exploited in attacks
articles.context: Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to...
articles.full_text:
SonicWall has released security updates to fix seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868, allows attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls, potentially including SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA).

The flaw has a CVSS severity score of 7.1 and only affects SonicOS SSL-VPN services configured to use SAML authentication.

In a security advisory published Friday, SonicWall warned that it had investigated a report that the vulnerability was exploited in an attack and urged customers to install the latest security updates.

"SonicWall PSIRT has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability. Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks," the company warned.

Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office discovered and reported the vulnerability.

While SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

CISA ordered federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected systems by November 20, 2026.

The advisory also fixes six additional vulnerabilities in SonicOS, including two management interface flaws rated 8.8 severity that allow unauthenticated attackers to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

The remaining flaws include pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL-VPN and TACACS+ services that could cause denial-of-service conditions, and a weak password hashing vulnerability affecting virtual appliances.

The vulnerabilities affect SonicOS Gen7 versions 7.3.3-7015 and earlier and Gen8 versions 8.2.2-8015 and earlier. SonicWall fixed the issues in versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 and says no workarounds are available.

The warning comes after a series of attacks targeting SonicWall's SMA1000 secure remote access appliances.

In October, security researchers detected exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to access internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to deploy malware on vulnerable appliances.

articles.title: Free Certified Patch for Critical Rails Active Storage Vulnerability
articles.context: Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary...
articles.full_text:
Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to a server through crafted uploads. Under certain configurations, attackers may also be able to read sensitive files, potentially leading to remote code execution.

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for the critical vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The patch is available to everyone, including developers and organizations that are not Socket customers, providing an additional remediation option for teams that cannot immediately upgrade Rails.

Impact #

The vulnerability affects Rails applications that use ImageMagick to process Active Storage attachments. ImageMagick supports multiple file format handlers, known as coders, some of which can access files outside the uploaded image. Active Storage did not restrict these coders, potentially allowing an attacker to invoke dangerous operations through a crafted upload.

Active Storage automatically analyzes files when they are attached, so exploitation does not require a separate preview, image transformation, or explicit analysis request.

According to the Rails advisory, applications are vulnerable when all three conditions are present:

Active Storage uses ImageMagick through config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick.

The system's ImageMagick security policy does not already block the dangerous coders.

The application accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

An attacker exploiting the vulnerability may be able to write arbitrary files on the server. Applications using Active Storage's Disk service may also expose files readable by the application process, including secret_key_base, application credentials, and database secrets. These disclosures could enable remote code execution or access to connected systems.

Upgrade Ruby on Rails #

The Rails team released versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 on November 4, 2026, and strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. These releases address the critical Active Storage vulnerability along with the other 20 security issues disclosed in the same update.

To upgrade, update the Rails version in your application's Gemfile to the appropriate patched release. For example, applications upgrading to Rails 8.1.4.1 can use:

gem "rails", "8.1.4.1"

Applications remaining on the 8.0 series should use 8.0.5.2.

Then update the dependencies with Bundler:

bundle update rails

Applications using the :mini_magick variant processor must also use MiniMagick 5.1 or later. Update the dependency if necessary and verify that the resolved version meets this requirement. Earlier MiniMagick versions will cause affected applications to raise an exception during boot after applying the Rails fix.

The updated Rails releases include a restrictive ImageMagick security policy that blocks dangerous coders and delegates. Applications that use ImageMagick for PDF or PostScript processing may need additional configuration adjustments.

Rails versions older than 8.0 are no longer supported. Security support for Rails 8.0 also ends on November 7, 2026, so teams should plan to move to the supported 8.1 series.

For additional instructions, see the official Ruby on Rails upgrade guide.

Free Socket Certified Patch Available #

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9, the critical Active Storage vulnerability that can allow arbitrary file writes and reads through malicious uploads.

Apply it with:

socket patch add GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9

Socket Certified Patches apply minimal, human-reviewed and AI-validated changes directly to vulnerable dependency versions, preserving the rest of the package's behavior. Patches are human-readable and can be reviewed before deployment.

The patch is available at no cost to anyone who needs it, whether or not they are a Socket customer. Making critical security fixes freely accessible is part of Socket's commitment to protecting the broader open source community and the developers and organizations that depend on it.

Certified Patches give teams time to plan and test upstream upgrades without leaving known vulnerabilities unaddressed. They are intended as an interim remediation option, with upgrading to a supported, patched Rails release remaining the recommended long-term solution.

This Certified Patch addresses GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 specifically, not the other vulnerabilities fixed in the November 4 Rails releases.

Recommended Actions #

Developers and organizations using Ruby on Rails should:

Upgrade Rails to 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2 as soon as possible, with a plan to move to a supported release series.

Verify MiniMagick compatibility and update to version 5.1 or later if the application uses :mini_magick.

Review Active Storage configurations to determine whether the application processes untrusted uploads through ImageMagick and whether its security policy blocks dangerous coders.

Apply Socket's free Certified Patch if an immediate Rails upgrade is not practical, then complete the upstream upgrade when possible.

Rotate potentially exposed credentials for applications using Active Storage's Disk service, as recommended in the Rails security advisory.

The official Rails security releases remain the recommended long-term fix. Socket's free Certified Patch gives teams an additional option to address the critical vulnerability without leaving affected applications exposed while upgrades are underway.

articles.title: OpenAI's new GPT-6 Cyber AI finds 81 Firefox flaws, 948 Linux bugs
articles.context: In October, researchers from OpenAI, Calif, and Wiz used AI models to discover two critical PHP vulnerabilities, dubbed PHP2Shell, which attackers began targeting even before...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has revealed GPT-6 Cyber, a new artificial intelligence model that has discovered 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel flaws.

The company announced the model on Thursday, saying it significantly improves on earlier AI models in finding software vulnerabilities, validating their impact, and helping developers create fixes.

During security testing, GPT-6 Cyber discovered 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and helped develop patches, many of which Mozilla has already released.

In separate Linux kernel research, the model identified 2,308 potential security flaws, successfully reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and developed local privilege escalation exploits for 948 distinct vulnerabilities that could allow an unprivileged user to gain root access.

In benchmark testing, GPT-6 Cyber successfully exploited 48.5% of vulnerabilities in ExploitGym, compared with 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.

OpenAI has classified the new model as having "Critical" cybersecurity capabilities under its Preparedness Framework, up from the "High" classification given to its previous model.

The new model is not publicly available, with access currently restricted to a select group of approved customers in OpenAI's Daybreak Red. OpenAI plans to expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon.

Daybreak Red supports advanced exploit development and authorized security testing, while the company's Daybreak Blue program allows verified defenders to investigate vulnerabilities and validate fixes with fewer restrictions.

OpenAI warned that defenders have a limited window to use increasingly powerful AI models to discover and patch vulnerabilities before similar capabilities become more widely available to attackers.

"It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software," OpenAI said.

Recent research and breaches illustrate how AI is already accelerating vulnerability discovery and cyberattacks.

In October, researchers from OpenAI, Calif, and Wiz used AI models to discover two critical PHP vulnerabilities, dubbed PHP2Shell, which attackers began targeting even before security patches were released.

This week, a security researcher revealed that they used AI agents to conduct approximately 17,600 authentication tests and discover a previously unknown OpenSSH authentication bypass flaw known as '*sshole.'

Artificial intelligence is also increasingly being used to automate cyberattacks, with autonomous AI agents demonstrating the ability to compromise real-world systems.

In August, nearly 700 rogue agents powered by an OpenAI model escaped a controlled testing environment and exploited vulnerabilities to compromise Hugging Face infrastructure.

More recently, Chinese hackers used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against more than 200 organizations worldwide, compromising at least nine.

OpenAI said it plans to expand its Daybreak programs to bring advanced cybersecurity research tools to organizations of all sizes, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.

Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss.

Adaptive Security's AI agents analyze email intent, context, and behavior to uncover phishing, business email compromise, and invoice fraud.

See what's getting through with a 14-day read-only scan of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, with no MX changes.

Start your free email security scan.

articles.title: Installing the Fix for an Exploited WordPress Flaw Can Expose Some Sites One Last Time
articles.context: Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it
articles.full_text:
Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it.

The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it.

An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities earlier this week.

WordPress released the fix last week in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7, all listed in its security advisory.

The fix gives the temporary folder a random name. But the update that installs the fix unpacks its files using the old code already on the site, as WordPress's updater code shows. On sites running 5.9 or later, that old code names the folder after the downloaded file, so the name can be predicted one last time.

Before the fix, an attacker could use the installer to write a new configuration file, wp-config.php, into the temporary copy. The update would then overwrite the site's real file with that file. The part of the fix that stops this already works during the update that installs it, because WordPress copies the files into place using the new code.

An attacker who catches the window during that update can still set up the temporary copy of WordPress with their own database, log in to it, and run PHP code with the web server's permissions before the copy is deleted, Bayram says in his technical write-up. From there, the attacker can read or write files in the live WordPress site.

Who Is Exposed During the Update

Not every update exposes the installer, the researcher says. Complete packages always include the installer files. A smaller partial package, built for one specific starting version, exposes a site only if it happens to contain them.

On sites that allow automatic background updates, WordPress installs the fix automatically, via the same updater and the same steps.

The Hacker News checked WordPress.org's update service today for several versions. For updates within a branch, such as from 7.1.3 to 7.1.4, it offered a partial package, including for automatic updates. For a move from an older branch, such as from 7.0.7 to 7.1.4, it offered only complete packages.

On 4.4 through 5.8, the old code adds random characters to the folder's name. That hides the name unless the site leaks it some other way, such as in an error message, the researcher says.

Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one.

What to Do Before Updating

The researcher's first recommendation is to stop the web server from serving wp-content/upgrade at all. WordPress works with that folder directly on disk, so blocking web access does not break updates, he says.

Block the folder in the web server configuration. On Nginx, add location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }. On Apache, add Require all denied inside a <Directory> block for that folder in the virtual host configuration.

If you can only edit .htaccess, add RedirectMatch 403 ^/wp-content/upgrade/ to the .htaccess file in the WordPress root, above the WordPress rewrite rules.

Do not put an .htaccess file inside wp-content/upgrade itself. The old updater deletes everything in that folder before it unpacks an update, so the file would be gone when it is needed.

Confirm that a request to /wp-content/upgrade/ returns a 403 error.

Update to 7.1.4 or to the fixed release for your branch.

The other safe route, he says, is a manual update done outside the web root, the folder the web server serves. Back up the site files and database, unpack the new release in a folder the web server does not serve, copy the core files into place without touching wp-config.php or wp-content, and then run the WordPress database update. This way, no temporary installer is ever created in a folder the web can reach.

WP-CLI's wp core update command is no substitute, because it runs the same updater and unpacks the package into the same folder.

WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates, so there is no fix for them. The researcher says the flaw goes back to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008, and that those sites should move to a supported version.

Attacks and What to Check

CISA's catalog addition earlier this week was based on evidence of active exploitation, but the agency did not describe the attacks.

Wordfence, the WordPress security company that assigned the CVE identifier, saw attack attempts begin nine minutes after it deployed a firewall rule for the flaw on the day of the release. Two of the busiest sources kept checking small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which the company says, in its attack analysis, aligns with attempts to catch the moment a site updates.

Its score for the flaw in the CVE record is 8.1 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. In its lab tests, the window lasted only seconds. WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low.

Code that its authors describe as an exploit for the flaw has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week. One of them says its code also works on sites that still use a predictable folder during complete-package updates. Whether the code works has not been established.

For sites that stayed on an affected version after the release, Wordfence suggests looking for:

unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade

administrator accounts no one recognizes

plugins no one installed

PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there

Update

Bayram told The Hacker News on November 6 that whether a partial update is exposed depends on what that specific package contains. A partial package holds only the files that changed between two releases. If those do not include the installer files, the temporary copy cannot run as a WordPress installation, and the installer never becomes reachable.

A site also does not always get a partial package when one exists. WordPress falls back to a complete package if the site's core files do not match the official checksums or if the update is a reinstall.

The deciding factor, the researcher said, "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed."

articles.title: Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot
articles.context: Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

Image Source: Safe Security

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."

articles.title: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days
articles.context: Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to...
articles.full_text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Anthropic adds security center, admin controls to Claude Enterprise

Anthropic has rolled out additional security and administration capabilities for Claude Enterprise, including a security center (in beta) that checks an organization’s Claude configuration for chat, Cowork and Claude Code against settings Anthropic recommends. Inference hooks, now generally available, route prompts and tool calls to an organization’s existing data loss prevention and security tools for inspection, while a centralized console (also in beta) lets companies handle single sign-on, SCIM and other settings across all their Claude organizations from one place.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Fake OpenAI and SpaceX event invites phish Microsoft and Google accounts

Push Security has documented a phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events, which dangle rewards such as three months of ChatGPT Pro or Grok Heavy to get marketing employees to sign in with their work accounts. The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform. Push links the operator, with medium-high confidence, to earlier fake Zoom event pages and says the campaign relies on Google and Zapier short links, Cloudflare challenges and domains swapped out every few weeks to avoid detection.

Chainalysis breach also exposed password hashes and tokens

Chainalysis has widened its breach disclosure, saying it discovered on November 2 that names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users had been exposed, after initially reporting that only non-sensitive data was accessed. The company has since taken several products offline, including its KYT transaction monitoring service after detecting abnormal activity, and is reaching out to customers whose KYT accounts show signs of unauthorized access.

Google hands Agent Substrate, gVisor to CNCF for sandboxing AI agents

Google is donating Agent Substrate, an open source orchestration layer on top of Kubernetes for running large numbers of isolated AI agent sessions, and gVisor, its open source application kernel, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as Sandbox projects. When an agent goes idle, Agent Substrate saves its state to storage and can bring it back in under 500 milliseconds. gVisor handles system calls in user space so that untrusted, AI-generated code doesn’t interact directly with the host kernel. According to Google, placing both projects under the CNCF gives the community a shared, vendor-neutral base for agent infrastructure that can run on any Kubernetes cluster meeting conformance standards.

‘Hello’ messages hide Chinese-language attack framework targeting Flowise

Era researchers have detailed Greeter, a Chinese-language exploitation framework that bombarded Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only “hello” while abusing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute commands. The framework mapped the host, queried cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and tested whether it could run payloads from memory. Era counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, and of those whose version it could identify, 703 lacked authentication and 46 appeared to share the vulnerable setup used in its honeypots.

LLM Mixers turn hijacked enterprise AI access into underground business

Mandiant says it investigated several LLMJacking cases this year in which attackers took over companies’ access to AI models, generating fraudulent bills of more than $100,000 in a day and as much as $1 million in total at some organizations. Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to upgrade ordinary keys to full admin credentials. Google Threat Intelligence Group also found hijacked access being sold through so-called LLM Mixers, including the Jet Night token routing service, which it believes uses stolen keys to offer unlimited plans with claimed frontier model access for around $60 a month.

CryptoBilis-sold Trezor allegedly fitted with seed-stealing implant

Trezor is telling customers who bought its hardware wallets from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to transfer their funds to a freshly created wallet with a new seed, after a buyer reported finding an implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from the former Southeast Asian reseller, which also sold Ledger devices that were found to have been tampered with. According to the report, which Trezor has not yet verified, an added circuit board fitted with a cellular module and antenna captures the recovery phrase displayed on screen and transmits it over a mobile network whenever the device is connected. No stolen funds have been reported.

Harvard alumni and donor data from 2025 breach added to HIBP

Have I Been Pwned has loaded roughly 851,000 unique email addresses from Harvard University’s November 2025 breach, an incident subsequently tied to a ShinyHunters extortion bid. The records come from Harvard’s alumni and fundraising systems and contain detailed profiles of donors, alumni and parents, as well as some faculty, staff and students, including names, contact details, birth dates and places, employers, ethnicities, marital statuses and donation histories.

SAP exploitation window shrinks to days as ransomware interest grows

Onapsis and Recorded Future report that for SAP vulnerabilities patched in 2025 and 2026, the median gap between a security note’s release and the first verified exploitation or public proof-of-concept was one to three days, down from 489 days for flaws patched in 2021. Ransomware and extortion groups showing up in SAP-related content grew from 8 in 2023 to 26 in 2025, and SAP CVEs with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation or public proof-of-concept code doubled from 9 to 18 between the end of 2023 and mid-2026. The study, drawing on over 1.2 million threat intelligence events, also tracked underground listings for SAP access priced from $500 to $30,000.

Synology flaw patched in 2024 now exploited in ransomware attacks

Synology warns that attackers are abusing a vulnerability fixed in December 2024 to hit devices still running outdated DSM releases, with the goal of encrypting data and extorting victims. The company has not identified the specific flaw beyond pointing to its Synology-SA-24:20 advisory. Synology recommends that anyone on a vulnerable release update DSM right away and turn on automatic updates.

Alleged Nomad Bridge exploiter appears in US court after extradition

Alexander Gurevich, a 49-year-old Israeli national now known as Alexander Block, appeared in a US court for the first time on October 30, a day after Israel extradited him to face charges that he exploited the Nomad Bridge smart contract in August 2022 to take virtual currency worth roughly $2.89 million. According to the indictment, he swapped the stolen WBTC and WETH for other cryptocurrencies and spread them across multiple addresses to obscure their origin. The money laundering charge alone carries a maximum of 20 years in prison.

articles.title: Metasploit Wrapup: Unauth RCE modules in Network Perimeter Devices and much more

articles.full_text:
Buckle up Metasploit-Framework enthusiasts because we have another action packed release for you. I'm talking, unauthenticated remote code execution modules in some of the biggest names in network perimeter devices like Citrix NetScaler and Cisco Secure Email Gateway. That's not all, we have an authenticated GitLab CI/CD regular expression integer overflow RCE module that was recently making head lines among many other awesome exploit modules. Looking for auxiliary modules? We've got you covered this release with a Flowise authentication bypass and a OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 hash disclosure, because who doesn't love collecting and cracking (or in some cases relaying) NTLM hashes am I right or am I right? In our continued effort to expand the payloads supported by the framework this week we saw fetch payload support for LoongArch. Lastly, if you're ever on an engagement or at home doing some testing and you see something that's not supported in Metasploit-Framework that you'd like to see supported, either drop us suggested-features issue on GitHub or trying throwing up a Pull Request, we'd love to hear from you. Happy hacking everyone!

New module content (13)

Flowise Authentication Bypass

Authors: Arthur Gervais, Isaac David, and Richard Howe

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21757 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: admin/http/flowise_auth_bypass_cve_2025_58434

CVE reference: CVE-2025-58434

Description: Adds a new auxiliary module that exploits CVE-2025-58434, an unauthenticated account takeover in Flowise versions 3.0.5 and earlier. Flowise's password reset API returns a valid reset token directly in its response, so the module can reset the password of any account whose email address is known, with no credentials needed.

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21865 contributed by jvoisin

Path: admin/http/spip_idor_password_reset

Description: This adds an auxiliary module which exploits a vulnerability in SPIP before 4.4.23 which allows attackers to change any user's password given a validly-signed POST without checking that the caller is authorized for that id_auteur. This issue was patched in 4.4.23 although no CVE has been assigned at the time of writing.

HashiCorp Consul Version Scanner

Author: h00die

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #22010 contributed by h00die

Path: scanner/http/hashicorp_consul_version

Description: Adds Hashicorp Consul version scanner.

OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 Hash Disclosure via UNC Path Proxy Source

Pull request: #21541 contributed by vognik

CVE-2026-25856: A Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploit that abuses the plain C# execution mode to run arbitrary .NET APIs and access the file system. CVE-2026-39908: A credential disclosure scanner for Windows that forces the app to reveal the NTLMv2 hash by loading a malicious UNC path. Both vulnerabilities affect OpenBullet2 releases starting from version 0.2.5.

Citrix NetScaler Unauthenticated Login Log Command Injection (CVE-2026-88771)

Portainer Authenticated Docker API Remote Root

Author: Aman Singh Gill (Gill-Singh-A)

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21745 contributed by Gill-Singh-A

Path: linux/http/portainer_authenticated_docker_rce

Description: Adds an exploit module that uses valid Portainer credentials and access to a managed Docker environment to create a privileged container, bind-mount the host filesystem, and execute a native Linux or Unix command payload as root on the underlying Docker host. The module optionally pulls the required container image and removes temporary containers after payload execution.

Linux ELF Executable Payload Injection Persistence

Author: dledda-r7

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21839 contributed by dledda-r7

Description: This adds a new Linux ELF injector persistence module supporting x86, x64, and AArch64 architectures to enable payload injection and persistence. The tool uses code cave and segment injection techniques alongside architecture-specific trampolines to seamlessly preserve original execution flow.

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #22017 contributed by jheysel-r7

Path: multi/http/gitlab_cicd_regexp_rce_cve_2026_97229

CVE reference: CVE-2026-97229

Description: Adds an exploit module for CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in GitLab’s CI/CD regular expression compiler that can lead to remote command execution as the git user. The module targets affected official GitLab CE/EE Linux amd64 releases, requires credentials with write access to a public project, and uses the unauthenticated CI lint API for payload delivery. Temporary branches and personal access tokens are automatically removed after exploitation.

articles.title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
articles.context: Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service...
articles.full_text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.

These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.

While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.

The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).

"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.

"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."

Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.

D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.

In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.
