articles.title: Hackers Exploit Patched Apple Flaw to Deliver Info-Stealing Malware, CISA Says
articles.context: The addition of CVE-2024-27834 to the KEV catalog follows a report from Sekoia that threat actors possibly linked to Russia exploited previously patched vulnerabilities in...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a medium-severity security flaw impacting multiple Apple operating systems to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2024-27834 (CVSS score: 5.5), a case of improper authentication that could allow an attacker with arbitrary read and write capability to bypass Pointer Authentication.

It was addressed by Apple in May 2024 with improved checks in iOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 16.7.8, iOS 17.5 and iPadOS 17.5, macOS Sonoma 14.5, tvOS 17.5, watchOS 10.5, and Safari 17.5. The vulnerability was demonstrated as a zero-day at the Pwn2Own Vancouver hacking contest held in March that year.

The addition of CVE-2024-27834 to the KEV catalog follows a report from Sekoia that threat actors possibly linked to Russia exploited previously patched vulnerabilities in Safari and Google Chrome to deliver malware capable of harvesting browser and device data.

The activity has been attributed to APT29 (aka Cozy Bear and Midnight Blizzard), a state-sponsored hacking group affiliated with Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, with "moderate to high confidence."

The attacks involve three initial access pathways – compromised legitimate websites, fake sites masquerading as popular websites, and a supply chain attack aimed at Plerdy SEO Tracker – to serve malicious JavaScript that triggers the vulnerability and ultimately deploy the information-stealing payload after profiling the visitor's device.

The zero-click exploit chain combines CVE-2025-43529, a remote code execution flaw in WebKit, and CVE-2025-43529, the pointer authentication codes (PACs) bypass, to execute a JavaScript payload designed for browser cookie theft.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the necessary patches by November 18, 2026.

articles.title: Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers
SonicWall Won't Patch EoL GMS Flaws That Could Expose Files, Alter Database Records
articles.context: The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from...
articles.full_text:
SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched.

Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below -

CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information.

CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions.

"The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert.

"As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

articles.title: APT29-Linked Hackers Hijack Web Analytics Script to Deliver iOS and Android Exploits
articles.context: 7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft
articles.full_text:
The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker.

"The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android."

The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026.

A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors -

Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript

Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria

Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js"

Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort.

"It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said.

"However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites."

Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data.

On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified -

Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft.

Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive.

Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords.

In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated.

AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671.

"This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation."

Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve

The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live."

The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding.

"It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing."

The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7.

"These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device."

Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network.

According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026.

Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns.

In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system.

"Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain."

"The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

articles.title: The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
articles.context: This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail
articles.full_text:
One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.

Today, I noticed a slight resurgence in scans targeting e-mail scripts on our honeypots. Today, there are numerous scripts like the old "formail" scripts, and it is hard to link a specific vulnerability to any of these scans. But my main suspect is spammers looking for webforms that allow setting arbitrary "To" headers. The URLs I am seeing:

"/sendmail.php" "/test-mail.php" "/testemail.php" "/config/mail_config.php" "/mail_config.php" "/email-test.php" "/mailtest.php"

In particular, the "Test" part of the filename suggests that the attacker is not looking for production scripts, but for test scripts left behind during development. This, along with the requests for credential/secret files that top our "Leaderboard," points to a more fundamental issue: Code hygiene. Do not leave behind development artifacts that should never have reached a live website.

For example, some excerpts from a random "mailtest.php" script that came back in a Google search [mailtest]:

<?php

/* DONT FORGET TO DELETE THIS SCRIPT WHEN FINISHED! */

$server = array( 'HTTP_HOST', 'SERVER_NAME', 'SERVER_ADDR', 'SERVER_PORT', 'SERVER_ADMIN', 'SERVER_SIGNATURE', 'SERVER_SOFTWARE', 'REMOTE_ADDR', 'DOCUMENT_ROOT', 'REQUEST_URI', 'SCRIPT_NAME', 'SCRIPT_FILENAME', ); $to = ( isset( $_GET['email'] ) ? $_GET['email'] : FALSE ); $subject = 'Mail Test Successful for ' . $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']; $message = '';

??????? foreach ( $server as $s ) { $message .= sprintf( '%s: %s', $s, $_SERVER[$s] ) . PHP_EOL; };

$success = mail( $to, $subject, $message, $headers );

The comment at the top says it all: This is not meant for production use, and even on a development site, it should likely be deployed only briefly for debugging. The script takes any "To" address from the "email" GET parameter and exfiltrates/displays part of the server configuration. It can be useful to scan your own hosts for some of these URLs as an additional control, but you really want to catch these issues during application deployment.

[CVE] https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2000-0411 [mailtest] https://gist.github.com/Porrapat/60ed7411d933122fc481

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

articles.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
articles.context: If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it
articles.full_text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

CVE-2026-121156: Buffer overflow in Dawn.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a block of memory than it can hold. This can cause a crash or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run code.

articles.title: Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
articles.context: A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads...
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read.

Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems.

Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier.

ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit.

The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze.

An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script.

Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited.

The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security.

Which Rails Apps Are Affected

An app is affected only if all three of these are true:

It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier.

Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not.

It accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants.

Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them.

In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one.

The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension.

Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it.

What to Do

Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy. MiniMagick is the Ruby gem Active Storage uses to call ImageMagick. In its default setup, every ImageMagick command it runs applies the policy, not only commands from Active Storage.

The policy blocks the MSL coder; coders that read or delete files other than the image; coders that fetch remote or local references or display them on a screen; every coder backed by Ghostscript, along with the gs delegate; and @filename indirection.

Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2. Apps on :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or later, or they raise an error at boot. Rails 8.0 gets security fixes only until November 7, 2026, under its maintenance policy.

Confirm that the app loads the new policy, as the Active Storage guide describes, by running bin/rails runner 'puts MiniMagick.identify { |i| i.list "policy" }'.

Check whether the shipped policy reaches the app at all. It does not reach an app that replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clears the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or installs its own MiniMagick::Shell. Such an app must put the rules in ImageMagick's system policy.

Apps that use GraphicsMagick get no protection from the shipped policy, because GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.

Check the server's own ImageMagick policy. The shipped policy adds to it rather than replacing it. A rule there that allows a coder, including a wildcard such as pattern="*", overrides the shipped policy's block on that coder.

If the app renders PDF or PostScript files through ImageMagick, re-allow the gs delegate and the coders it uses in the server's policy.xml.

If you cannot upgrade yet, copy the rules of the shipped policy, activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml, into ImageMagick's system policy, such as /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Rails also published the fix as patches for 8.1 and 8.0.

Apps on release series older than 8.0 can use that workaround or upgrade to 8.0 or later.

Rails' workarounds for the second flaw only change how FFmpeg is used. None of them covers ImageMagick.

If the app stores attachments with the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every other secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not keep an exposed secret as a fallback.

The advisory does not explain how to check whether an app has already been targeted.

articles.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
articles.context: " Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs
articles.full_text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

articles.title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
articles.context: “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place
articles.full_text:
Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild.

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live.

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this.

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED.

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed.

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

articles.title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
articles.context: Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication
articles.full_text:
IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

articles.title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
articles.context: Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level...
articles.full_text:
You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.

AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.

To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.

How it works

Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.

Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.

We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer.

Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.

Our focus

Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.

We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.

A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.

A walk through Zero Wire

Start on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.

Find what needs attention

The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.

The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.

Understand what happened and who should investigate

When you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.

For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.

Turn the briefing into an action plan

What to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.

The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.

Assess your exposure with an AI agent

In this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.

Check the evidence and follow what changed

To help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity.

If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.

Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.

Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.

Understand Cloudflare’s role

The Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure.

If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.

Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.

Stay informed with Zero Wire

A useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.

Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.

Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

articles.title: Red Hat Patches 9.8-Rated Linux TCP RCE Flaw While Ubuntu Releases Fixes for Testing
articles.context: Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its...
articles.full_text:
Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its three newest long-term-support releases remain in its opt-in testing channel with no date for a regular update.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, can be reached by a remote, unauthenticated attacker and can lead to remote code execution, Red Hat and Canonical said.

The Linux kernel's own CVE team rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Red Hat, which initially rated it Moderate at 5.9, has raised its score to 9.8 and now calls it Critical. The bug has been present since Linux 4.4, and the upstream fix landed in October.

What the Flaw Is

When a server accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, the kernel passes IP options from the incoming request to the new socket without copying them. If the client retransmits its connection request while another processor still reads those options, the kernel can read memory it has already freed.

An attacker triggers the race by sending connection requests that carry IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options to any listening TCP port. No login is needed. IPv6 is not affected on the main path.

Red Hat shipped RHSA-2026:93414 (RHEL 8), RHSA-2026:93412 (RHEL 9), and RHSA-2026:93413 (RHEL 10) on November 1. A reboot is needed after installing the update.

RHEL Version

Fixed Kernel

Errata

8.10

4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10

RHSA-2026:93414

9.8

5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8

RHSA-2026:93412

10.2

6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2

RHSA-2026:93413

Canonical said on November 2 that fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 26.04 LTS are in its -proposed pocket, an opt-in testing channel. Packages there do not install automatically.

Canonical tests kernel updates across more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before releasing them to the regular update channel, and no release date has been given.

Ubuntu Release

-proposed Kernel

Status

22.04 LTS (Jammy)

5.15.0-203.213

In -proposed

24.04 LTS (Noble)

Pending

Administrators who need the fix before it reaches the regular channel can enable -proposed and install the kernel update by running:

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade sudo reboot

To check whether a system is running a fixed kernel, compare the output of uname -r against the versions in the tables above.

Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 have no fix yet. Older releases require Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro.

Cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernel variants for Ubuntu are listed as work in progress on the Ubuntu CVE page with target versions, but Canonical's blog post covers only the generic kernel.

Interim Mitigation

Red Hat published an nftables rule on October 30 that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. The rule blocks the known trigger for the race but cannot fully prevent exploitation and may break workloads that depend on IPv4 options, Red Hat said.

table inet cve_2026_98432 { chain input { type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept; ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop } }

The filter applies only to the host where it is loaded. Traffic between containers on the same host can bypass it, a member of the CIQ kernel team noted on the oss-security mailing list.

Several sources have recommended disabling Multipath TCP (MPTCP) as a workaround. The flaw is in the IPv4 TCP path, not in MPTCP, and that advice alone is not enough, Canonical said. "The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation."

Exploitation Status

No vendor, CERT, or the kernel CVE team has reported attacks using this flaw. It was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's October 30 release.

Anthropic said on October 27 that an unreleased, internal Claude research model wrote a remote root exploit for the flaw that works against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, with no credentials and no user interaction. In its proof of concept, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes and reaching a root shell took another 5 minutes. Anthropic has not published the exploit code.

Proof-only code that triggers the race and detects the kernel echoing freed memory in a SYN-ACK has appeared on GitHub. It does not implement code execution.

Amazon Linux scored the flaw 8.1 and rated it Important, saying the main outcome is a crash with possible memory corruption. Debian, Oracle Linux, and SUSE shipped fixes in October. Amazon Linux was fixed across all packages between October 24 and 30.

articles.title: Synology NAS Devices Targeted in Ransomware Attacks Exploiting Patched DSM Flaw
articles.context: The Taiwanese vendor said it observed threat actors exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to target devices running outdated versions of DSM
articles.full_text:
Synology is urging customers to update the DiskStation Manager (DSM) software powering its Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices following ransomware attacks.

The Taiwanese vendor said it observed threat actors exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to target devices running outdated versions of DSM.

"These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom," it said in a statement released last week.

While Synology did not disclose the exact security flaw that's being exploited in these attacks, the company linked to a November 2024 security advisory that listed three vulnerabilities -

CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in the system plugin daemon of DSM that could lead to remote code execution via unspecified vectors.

CVE-2024-50629 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in the webapi component of DSM that could allow remote attackers to read limited files via unspecified vectors.

CVE-2024-10445 (CVSS score: 4.3) - An improper certificate validation vulnerability in the update functionality in DSM that could allow remote attackers to write limited files via unspecified vectors.

The issues were addressed in the following versions -

DSM 7.2.2 - Upgrade to 7.2.2-72806-1 or above

DSM 7.2.1 - Upgrade to 7.2.1-69057-6 or above

DSM 7.2 - Upgrade to 7.2-64570-4 or above

DSM 7.1 - Upgrade to 7.1.1-42962-7 or above

DSM 6.2 - Upgrade to 6.2.4-25556-8 or above

The development comes amid reports from customers that their Synology devices have been hit by C3RB3R ransomware, which has been observed locking users' files with a ".L0CK3D" extension.

In an analysis published last week, Chinese security vendor Qihoo 360 Internet Security Center said C3RB3R has a "long history" of deploying ransomware against NAS devices, including by exploiting two DSM vulnerabilities that were addressed by Synology back in September 2026 -

CVE-2026-13684 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in SCGI that could allow remote attackers to read or write arbitrary files and conduct denial-of-service attacks.

CVE-2026-13639 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An insufficient entropy vulnerability in login logic that could allow remote attackers to read or write arbitrary files and conduct denial-of-service attacks.

Once launched, C3RB3R scans files on the compromised device, while skipping 27 directories and certain extensions (e.g., BAT, DLL, EXE, LNK, MOD, MSI, and SYS) to avoid triggering system crashes and impacting its encryption process. Files that are successfully encrypted receive a .L0CK3D extension and a ransom note named "read-me3.txt" is dropped in each encrypted directory.

This is not the first time NAS devices have been the target of ransomware attacks. In 2019, NAS devices manufactured by Taiwan-based QNAP Systems were compromised by QNAPCrypt (aka eCh0raix) ransomware.

Then, in August 2021, Synology warned of brute-force attacks driven by a malware family called StealthWorker that led to ransomware infections.

"These attacks leverage a number of already infected devices to try and guess common administrative credentials, and if successful, will access the system to install its malicious payload, which may include ransomware," it said at the time. "Devices infected may carry out additional attacks on other Linux-based devices, including Synology NAS."

That same month, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 also disclosed details of an eCh0raix variant targeting NAS devices from both QNAP and Synology by leveraging vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-28799 or brute-force their way in by making use of commonly used administrative credentials.

"Synology strongly urges all users running vulnerable versions to update DSM immediately to protect their systems," the company said. "Synology also recommends enabling automatic updates to keep DSM up to date at all times."

articles.title: Attackers Target Unpatched CryptoPayment Gateway Flaw That Can Expose Wallet Credentials
articles.context: Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-81648, which carries a CVSS score of 10.0. Successful exploitation of the flaw could permit unauthenticated users to delete arbitrary files on the server and extract sensitive data, including stored wallet credentials.

"The CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin from 1.2.1 to 1.2.2 does not apply an authorization check on one of its AJAX endpoints, allowing unauthenticated users to invoke administrative operations, including deleting arbitrary files on the server, overwriting the payment gateway configuration and recovering stored wallet credentials in cleartext," according to a description of the flaw on the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The vulnerability affects versions 1.2.1 through 1.2.2, which is the latest version. There are no known fixes for the flaw, according to WP Scan. As of August 28, 2026, the plugin has been closed on the WordPress Plugin Directory and is no longer available for download due to an unspecified "security issue."

Statistics show that the plugin has been collectively downloaded 1,845 times, including 20 downloads over the last seven days. It's unclear if it's actively installed on any WordPress sites.

"We are observing in-the-wild exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-81648, a critical (CVSS 10.0) flaw in the CryptoPayment Gateway for WordPress," Defused Cyber said in an X post. "The attacks we recorded came from infrastructure that markets themselves as 'Anonymous KYC-Free VPS Hosting.'"

In the absence of a fix, site owners are advised to remove the plugin, rotate wallet keys, and audit for any suspicious changes.

articles.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
articles.context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
articles.full_text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

articles.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
articles.context: Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead,...
articles.full_text:
In this article

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Next in line

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

References

Learn More

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

articles.title: Armadin Tests Find 88% of Severe Flaws Outside Vendor Advisories
articles.context: Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or...
articles.full_text:
Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

articles.title: AI Vulnerability Finding
articles.context: Clive Robinson • November 2, 2026 11:45 AM @ Jeff, ALL, With regards, “More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more...
articles.full_text:
Clive Robinson • November 2, 2026 11:45 AM

@ Jeff, ALL,

With regards,

“More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more likely explanation is that the bugs were already there and now we’re closing them at the fastest pace in history! “

Actually both points are true…

Yes we are finding “new instances of bugs from known classes of bugs” at a much higher rate.

But that does not mean we are finding “new classes of bugs” (ie black swans).

But also “vibe coding” by AI is certainly generating “new instances of bugs” at a more alarming rate.

It’s why quite a few employers are now seeing “laying off humans with AI” as being not just horrifically unprofitable, but extremely dangerous to the business.

Yes, AI has niche advantages, but those niches are invariably not general in nature.

Even China is begining to see the dangers of even low cost AI.

None of this was unpredictable and quite a few have called it that way. However when you’ve handed over everything for a few tulip bulbs you had better be sure not only are they going to grow but that people are going to by the result sufficient to pay a “Return on Investment”(ROI).

Right now the ROI in “General AI” is not a certainty or even a likely hood based on the current economy…

Then there is “clearing up the mess of harms” the rush for AI has created… How many billions if not trillions that is going to cost companies that are already by normal forecasting methods “bankrupt”…

articles.title: Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527)
articles.context: Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3
articles.full_text:
Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

The following scores and classifications are from Ivanti's updated advisory:
