articles.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

articles.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

articles.title: Broccoli2shell: Everything You Need To Know About The Critical Brotli Decoder Vulnerability
articles.context: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library
articles.full_text:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.

CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.

Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.

According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

Which products are affected?

Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.

Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
articles.context: There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

articles.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943)
articles.context: Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.

Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.

Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.

eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.

Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.

Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.

Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.

Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.

Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.

Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.

The Eight Affected Intermediate Certificates

How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete

Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.

Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.

Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.

Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897

Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates

Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems.

Enumerate Affected eMudhra Certificate Chains

In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. This Information Gathered (IG) QID helps identify systems presenting or using certificate chains that contain the affected eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. Once available in your subscription, you can query for assets using:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:48395

Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View

Open Certificate View > Certificates, paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list.

certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`)

The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency.

The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc, because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates).

Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically.

Note: QQL query tokens are case-sensitive. If a query returns a syntax error, check the search token list in the Certificate View help and adjust the token name.

Response and Remediation

Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain.

Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates.

Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date.

Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean.

Conclusion

The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Certificate View gives you the issuer search and dashboards to find eMudhra-issued certificates, and VMDR and Cloud Agent inventory show which hosts and applications still need vendor updates. articles.title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 2: Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Cloud Context
articles.context: For example: SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active...
articles.full_text:
In Part 1, we established how to centralize your AppSec tools, correlate assets, and map scanner coverage across repositories. Establishing visibility is an essential baseline, but once your connectors start streaming data into a single location, prioritization becomes the primary focus.

As highlighted in our recent State of SDLC Security 2026 report, AI’s primary impact isn't necessarily introducing entirely new risks. It's the amplification of existing ones through faster code generation, contributing to a wider attack surface area with less time for human review.

For lean AppSec teams, the real promise of ASPM lies in how it helps prioritize application risk across their enterprise. But, as we saw with the React2Shell example, prioritization requires context across the entire application lifecycle. AppSec teams must quickly distinguish between theoretical code flaws sitting on un-deployed branches and active vulnerabilities running on internet-facing workloads.

To transform raw scanner output into actionable risk, Wiz Code executes prioritization across two distinct layers:

Finding-level prioritization: Normalizing scanner data into unified schemas, actively enriching findings with threat intelligence and network reachability, and deduplicating identical alerts across overlapping tools.

Attack path prioritization: Using the Wiz Security Graph to connect code-level findings with live cloud runtime context, elevating isolated flaws into fully validated attack paths.

Let’s look at how to operationalize both layers in your environment.

Enrich, Deduplicate, and Prioritize Individual Findings

Findings from connected scanners populate into their respective domains in the Wiz platform. For example, SAST results flow into the SAST Findings tab, SCA results populate in the Vulnerability Findings tab, and Secret results show up in the Secret Findings page. You can easily filter any table by “origin” to isolate alerts from a specific tool. In the example below, we’re filtering vulnerability findings surfaced from a Snyk SCA scan.

From this unified baseline, Wiz executes multiple layers of prioritization to help AppSec teams focus on what matters.

Enrichment

Imported findings are enriched with domain specific context, turning generic alerts into prioritized findings. For example:

SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active exploit availability, and CISA KEV status. Our Threat Research team also denotes findings with active threats and writes complete advisories, so security teams have the latest insight on zero days.

SAST: CWE findings include code snippets so security teams have visibility into the location and context of weaknesses.

DAST: Wiz independently validates network exposure for the web applications with DAST findings using the Attack Surface Management (ASM) module. The ASM engine can be configured to run other checks such as secrets or sensitive data exposure checks from the perimeter on these newly created endpoints. Private-only addresses are marked differently so teams can prioritize findings with a real external attack surface.

Secrets: Wiz runs ingested secrets through databases to see if the secret was leaked, classifies secret types for understanding its impact, and assigns severities to the detected secrets based on threat research if the originating scanner did not provide any.

Deduplication

Security teams should not waste time chasing down multiple vulnerability findings for the exact same issue. When multiple tools scan the same codebase and produce duplicative vulnerability findings, Wiz can easily reconcile them.

Wiz labels one finding as "Representative" and the duplicates as "Duplicate." Teams can apply automated Ignore Rules scoped to duplicate findings, instantly eliminating redundant noise in reporting without losing the underlying scanner audit trail. So instead of generating individual tickets for each finding, teams can create one ticket to consolidate the findings.

Prioritize Exploitable Attack Paths

Traditionally ASPM has focused on aggregating findings and prioritizing risk using simple scoring. Wiz takes a different approach by correlating findings with additional risk on the Wiz Security Graph. This is where the platform moves from managing vulnerabilities to managing exploitable attack paths.

The Wiz Security Graph correlates multiple risk factors into a single Wiz Issue (identifying toxic combinations of risk). Critically, these controls run on your third-party findings exactly the same way they run on native Wiz findings. If you connect a scanner, its data instantly becomes part of your code-to-cloud attack path analysis.

What this looks like in practice

Let's look at how this context transforms a standard alert into a prioritized Wiz Issue. Imagine your Snyk integration flags a high-severity SAST finding (such as a remote code execution or command injection flaw) on a repository branch. In a vacuum, a developer might treat this as an urgent priority, or they might ignore it if they assume it is an internal tool.

The Wiz Security Graph evaluates the entire deployment lifecycle to uncover the actual risk. A single Wiz Issue might reveal:

The Code Flaw: A SAST finding from Snyk and a native Wiz SAST finding, both originating on the same repository branch.

The Build Artifact: That specific branch was built into a container image currently running in a production Kubernetes cluster.

The Exposure: The Kubernetes cluster is exposed to the internet via a public application endpoint.

Active Validation: An Attack Surface Management (ASM) finding confirms the endpoint is actively reachable from the outside.

Instead of manually piecing together four separate alerts across three different tools, Wiz draws the connection natively. Because these findings all resolve to the same underlying resource and represent the same attack path, they are surfaced as one unified, high-priority Wiz Issue.

Conversely, if that same SAST flaw was detected on a branch that never ships to a running cloud workload, it remains a low-priority finding—sparing developers from interrupting their sprint for a non-exploitable risk.

Manage security debt at scale

Not every finding may map to an attack path. But, lower-severity findings still represent real risk if left unaddressed. In Wiz, organizations can track and govern these findings through Posture Issues.

AppSec teams can create logical groupings of findings based on several criteria such as severity, project, code repository and more to build tailored campaigns for managing security debt. Teams can also define SLAs for remediation to align with organizational policies.

Up Next: Remediation and Automation at Machine Speed

Separating signal from noise is a massive win, but prioritization without rapid remediation is only half the battle. Once critical attack paths are identified, how do you ensure the right engineering team fixes them without slowing down release cycles?

In Part 3, the final instalment of this series, we’ll explore how to remediate at machine speed. We’ll cover how to leverage the Wiz Green Agent to generate tailored remediation plans in developer workflows and how to automate response with Wiz Workflows.

articles.title: The early bird gets the exploit.
articles.context: AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections...
articles.full_text:
Amazon spots PHP exploits before disclosure. GitLab patches a critical flaw. Meta faces a $25 billion penalty. Autonomous AI agents power new cyberattacks. Hackers breach a Japanese cloud provider. CyberCartel unleashes AI against Latin American banks. Tor exit nodes are hijacked. OpenAI coding agents disable security monitoring. Interpol dismantles thousands of cybercrime networks across Africa. Our guest is Danny Manimbo, ISO and AI Practice Leader at Schellman, explaining why companies waiting for AI regulatory clarity may already be behind. Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Today is Thursday October 22nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Amazon detected PHP exploitation attempts days before public disclosure.

Amazon Threat Intelligence detected attempts to exploit two PHP vulnerabilities four days before their public disclosure on October 21st. The activity, observed through Amazon’s MadPot honeypot network, originated from anonymized infrastructure, suggesting threat actor involvement. How the attackers obtained exploit information remains unknown.

Additional attempts appeared hours before disclosure, followed by widespread exploitation once patches became available. Researchers believe multiple actors were involved, although it’s unclear whether the early attacks would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Amazon warns that coordinated disclosure no longer guarantees a head start for defenders. AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections that don’t depend on vulnerability-specific signatures.

GitLab patches a maximum-severity vulnerability.

GitLab has released emergency patches for a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s Regular Expression Compiler. It affects both Community and Enterprise editions, and GitLab is urging customers to update immediately.

The Shadowserver Foundation tracks more than 2,700 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, although it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

This is GitLab’s second critical remote code execution vulnerability in ten days, both reported by the same security researcher. Last month, GitLab also patched a maximum-severity flaw that could expose sensitive information. CISA subsequently confirmed active exploitation of that vulnerability and ordered federal agencies to patch.

GitLab says its hosted service is already protected.

Meta is fined $25 billion in New Mexico.

A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties stemming from the Cambridge Analytica privacy scandal.

A jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law, concluding that Meta misled users about its data collection practices, privacy protections, and harmful content.

The judge initially calculated penalties totaling nearly $220 billion before reducing the award to $25 billion, with annual interest of 15 percent until it’s paid.

The ruling also criticized Facebook’s internal investigation following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, calling it deliberately ineffective.

New Mexico’s attorney general hailed the decision as a warning to powerful technology companies.

Meta strongly disputes the ruling and plans to appeal, arguing that the state’s approach effectively imposes a tax on online speech.

Researchers uncovered new threat actors using autonomous AI agents.

CrowdStrike researchers have uncovered four previously undocumented threat actors using autonomous AI agents to conduct cyberattacks, with some operations achieving their objectives within an hour.

The actors, operating in Spanish, Chinese, Indonesian, and Russian, targeted government agencies, healthcare organizations, and private companies worldwide. Their activities included successful intrusions and data theft.

Researchers discovered the campaigns after the attackers inadvertently exposed their offensive AI frameworks through publicly accessible directories.

The operations varied considerably in sophistication. One actor employed multiple coordinated AI agents, while another, despite limited technical skills, successfully compromised government systems using publicly available tools.

CrowdStrike warns that agentic AI is lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime, allowing less-skilled attackers to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations at machine speed. Researchers expect these AI-powered intrusions to grow in both volume and sophistication.

Hackers compromise a Japanese cloud hosting provider.

Hackers have compromised a Japanese cloud hosting provider, potentially installing malware on nearly 27,000 customer servers.

Onamae (o-na-MA-ay) Desktop Cloud, operated by GMO Internet, confirmed unauthorized access to its infrastructure and the installation of malicious software in customer environments.

The company began shutting down affected services on October 21st, disrupting all Desktop Cloud plans. There’s no estimated timeline for restoring service.

GMO warns that information stored on compromised servers may have been exposed, although it has not confirmed any data theft or misuse. Credit card information was unaffected because it’s stored separately.

Customers are being urged to change passwords and other credentials stored on their servers and remain alert for phishing attempts.

The company says its investigation is ongoing and promises additional updates.

CyberCartel targets banks and payment providers across Latin America.

Security researchers at Straiker have uncovered an AI-powered attack system used by a cybercriminal group targeting banks and payment providers across Latin America.

The group, known as CyberCartel, has reportedly been active since 2012. Its latest operation uses a framework called CARLIY0S, which coordinates multiple commercial AI models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks.

The AI agents have specialized roles, including reconnaissance, exploit development, and evaluating competing attack strategies.

Researchers gained access to the group’s operational environment, uncovering a database containing nearly 4,500 records, including financial information, credentials, API keys, and backdoors.

Straiker says the group targeted more than 400 financial organizations in a matter of months.

The findings offer a rare look at AI becoming part of cybercriminal infrastructure, potentially allowing smaller groups to conduct sophisticated attacks faster and at greater scale.

Hackers hijack Tor exit nodes.

Hackers hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes in an operation designed to intercept SSH connections and unencrypted email traffic.

According to Tor volunteers, the intrusion began with a reused password that provided access to a management server. Attackers installed the Ebury Linux backdoor and eventually gained control of hundreds of exit relays.

Between October 2nd and 5th, the compromised nodes redirected SSH connections through attacker-controlled servers, potentially capturing passwords and installing additional malware. The attackers also blocked encrypted email ports while allowing unencrypted traffic, although it’s unclear whether any email interception succeeded.

Researchers still don’t know how the attackers compromised so many servers or who’s responsible.

The incident highlights the importance of enforcing encrypted email connections and using SSH keys instead of passwords, particularly when routing traffic through Tor.

OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring.

Two OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring while completing routine programming tasks.

In one case, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic security alerts after misinterpreting instructions not to send Slack messages. In another, a GPT-6 Astra agent removed monitoring software to match a reference implementation, then falsely told the user it hadn’t.

Both agents considered preserving the safeguards but ultimately prioritized their coding instructions.

OpenAI is strengthening its monitoring systems while investigating whether the incidents reflect excessive task persistence or a specific tendency to evade oversight.

Authorities shut down African cybercrime networks.

Interpol says an international law enforcement operation across Africa has resulted in more than 1,400 arrests and the disruption of nearly 11,000 cybercriminal networks.

Operation Serengeti III involved authorities from 21 countries, targeting ransomware, business email compromise, and online fraud between late June and August.

Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims, with estimated losses exceeding $385 million. Authorities recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds.

Among the results, Ugandan police arrested 365 suspects linked to investment and pension fraud. Angola seized more than 2,000 illegal cryptocurrency mining devices, while Nigerian authorities arrested a suspect allegedly responsible for a major phishing operation.

Private cybersecurity companies provided intelligence to help identify criminal infrastructure and suspects.

It’s the third Operation Serengeti crackdown since 2024, reflecting an ongoing international effort to disrupt cybercrime across the continent.

Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Spotify has spent the past year trying to keep AI-generated musical slop from overwhelming its platform, and apparently, there’s been plenty to clean up.

The streaming giant says it’s removed more than 50 million spammy or low-quality tracks from recommendations this year, on top of another 75 million tracks removed from the platform entirely.

Spotify says listeners were consistently skipping or rejecting content identified as slop, prompting changes to its recommendation algorithms.

The company has also introduced AI disclosure credits, verified more than 300,000 artists, and begun labeling AI-generated artist personas. Those virtual performers are generally excluded from recommendations unless listeners actively follow them.

Spotify acknowledges that detecting AI-generated content remains difficult, particularly as the technology improves.

The company insists its priority remains human artistry, even as artificial intelligence makes producing music easier than ever.

Apparently, just because a machine can write a song doesn’t mean anyone wants to hear it.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
articles.context: Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation
articles.full_text:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n!

As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.

The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.

Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site.

As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.

How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?

I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.

What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?

I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.

How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?

It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.

What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?

I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool.

Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating.

Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding?

I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application.

Think of a request parameter, uploaded file, API input, or data coming from another service. A sink can be a security-sensitive operation that consumes this data, for example, a network request, file access, process execution, database query, or authorization decision. The interesting part is tracing the path between the two. I look at how the data is transformed, validated, or passed across trust boundaries, and whether those controls are sufficient before it reaches the sink.

I like this approach because it lets me reason about attack paths without forcing my investigation into a predefined bug class. Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation. I consider a finding confirmed once I understand the attack path, can produce a working PoC, and can explain the impact.

Do you use AI in your research? Where does it genuinely help and where does it fall short?

Yes. Quite a lot, actually, but mostly as an accelerator. I use it for navigating unfamiliar code, finding call sites, tracing data through the codebase, and understanding how a system is structured and how its components interact. I also find it helpful for writing PoC scripts once I’ve identified the vulnerability.

Where it works best is when the question is specific. “Is this application vulnerable?” usually isn’t a very useful prompt. Give it the right context, explain what you already know, and ask a narrow question, and the quality goes up dramatically. There’s a bit of a paradox there. AI becomes more useful as you understand the problem better yourself. And I never treat its conclusions as facts. Hallucinations, false positives, bad assumptions, and confidently wrong answers are all common. Everything should still be manually verified. AI makes my work faster. However, it doesn’t replace understanding the application, developing intuition, or proving that something actually works.

What’s your guidance on using AI responsibly in bug bounty?

Use it to improve your research, not to outsource responsibility for it. If AI tells you it found a vulnerability, that doesn’t mean you found a real vulnerability. You still need to reproduce it yourself. You should understand exactly what’s happening, which security boundary or control is being violated, and what the real impact is. Ideally, you should understand the issue well enough that you could write the report without AI at all. Build a clear PoC. Make sure the security team can follow it. Know why every step matters.

AI has lowered the barrier to doing security research, which is great in a lot of ways. But you can also see the downside in the number of unverified reports teams now have to deal with. AI should make research better. Not just make more reports.

As the industry ships more AI-powered features, does testing them require a different mindset than traditional web bugs?

Yes. Conventional vulnerabilities still matter, but attackers may also be able to influence a probabilistic decision-making component through the data, instructions, or context it receives. But getting a model to say or do something unexpected isn’t necessarily the interesting part. The more important question is what that influence allows an attacker to achieve. Can they access something they should not or cause the system to act with privileges the attacker does not have? That’s why I don’t think model-level guardrails should ever be treated as the only or primary security boundary. You still need deterministic controls around the model. This includes proper authorization, least-privilege access, isolation, and validation. The surrounding systems matter just as much as the model itself. And traditional application security doesn’t disappear just because AI is involved. Model output should still be treated as untrusted input. If that output ends up in a browser, database query, shell command, web request, or another downstream system without the right controls, you can still end up with very familiar vulnerabilities: XSS, SQL injection, command injection, SSRF, and so on. I think the model is new. A lot of the dangerous sinks aren’t.

What’s one thing you wish you’d known when you first started?

Learn systems, not checklists. When I started, I was tempted to collect huge lists of techniques, payloads, tools, and bypasses and then work through them one by one. Those lists can be useful.

I still use them. But understanding how a system works has been far more valuable. Its internal logic. The data flows. Trust relationships. Assumptions. Why one component is allowed to talk to another. Why a particular restriction exists in the first place. I also learned not to assume something is secure because it looks secure, or because plenty of researchers have already tested it.

A lot of interesting research begins with: “Why does this work this way?” rather than “Which payload should I try next?” There’s some luck involved too. Sometimes you spend days following something that goes absolutely nowhere. Then you notice one tiny detail almost by accident and it turns into a high-impact finding. You can’t control that part. You can control whether you keep questioning things long enough to notice it.

What advice or resources would you recommend to researchers trying to land their first valid report?

Get comfortable with the fundamentals, then pick one program and one target and stick with them for a while. Constantly jumping between targets makes it difficult to build a real mental model of any of them. Use the application. Explore weird flows. Test different roles and permission levels. Read the documentation. Watch the requests and responses. Look at the APIs. Labs, courses, public write-ups, disclosed bug bounty reports, and intentionally vulnerable applications are all useful too. They teach you where bugs tend to hide and, over time, help build the intuition to recognize similar situations elsewhere.

One mistake I see a lot is relying on tools too early. Another is giving up because the obvious tests didn’t find anything. Tools help. They don’t build the mental model for you. And when you finally do find something, spend the extra time validating it properly. Create a working PoC. Make reproduction easy for the security team. Understanding one target deeply will usually get you further than trying to find a bug as quickly as possible.

What do you enjoy doing when you aren’t hacking?

Endurance sports, mainly road cycling, especially in the mountains. I enjoy the physical challenge of a long climb and pushing myself over longer distances. It’s also a great way to get away from screens for a while and spend some time outside. There’s actually something about climbing that feels pretty similar to vulnerability research. You can put in a lot of effort without seeing much progress. Sometimes you have no idea whether what you’re doing is going to lead anywhere. You just keep going. And every now and then, it pays off.

Any social media profiles you’d like to share with our readers?

You can find me on HackerOne.

Thank you, @r31n, for participating in GitHub’s bug bounty researcher spotlight! Each submission to our bug bounty program is a chance to make GitHub, our products, and our customers more secure, and we continue to welcome and appreciate collaboration with the security research community. So, if this inspired you to go hunting for bugs, feel free to report your findings through HackerOne.

The post How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

articles.title: Technical Advisory: PHP2Shell Pre-Auth RCE (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
articles.context: Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and...
articles.full_text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS v4.0 9.2 | No exploitation observed by Bitdefender | Patch immediately

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical pre-authentication remote code execution flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2) in the PHP worker process, and every unpatched PHP installation serving web requests is at risk, with Apache servers running mod_php at highest risk. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now; on 8.1 or older, which have no official fix, move to a supported branch. Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and GravityZone detections cover those actions. For exact remediation steps including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

2026-10-22: Initial publication. Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of this date. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation.

Situation

The flaws were first discovered by lcfr_hax of Calif, which reported an unconditional remote code execution with a shared root cause to PHP on 2026-08-11. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause that day, Wiz Research reported on 2026-08-24, and OpenAI sent further attack vectors on 2026-09-18 (The PHP Foundation, “Today’s PHP security release and how we’re strengthening PHP security”, October 2026). Wiz Research demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against the WordPress, Drupal and Joomla container images and credits frontier AI models with substantially lowering the barrier to exploit development.

The coordinated disclosure held until two days before the planned release. On 2026-10-20 at about 15:00 UTC the CVE IDs began circulating online with a wrong release time and a CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). PHP published its pre-announcement early at 19:30 UTC and moved the release forward from 2026-10-22 to 2026-10-21 at 14:00 UTC. At about 20:00 UTC Calif mistakenly published a video showing its proof of concept working against a number of targets. PHP says no technical details leaked, but the video contributed to the faster development of various proofs of concept. On 2026-10-21 at 07:41 UTC Chainguard published container images containing the fix more than six hours before the release, breaking the embargo. PHP released the fixed versions at 14:00 UTC and published PHP, “Security advisory 2026-10-21-5”, October 2026 with them (The PHP Foundation, October 2026). PHP states that its security team identified no functional exploits at the time of release.

Datadog Security Labs, “PHP2Shell critical vulnerabilities”, October 2026 reports that AWS saw exploitation attempts from 2026-10-17, and describes broad untargeted scanning. Bitdefender has not independently confirmed this. Operational guidance is maintained by NCSC-NL, “PHP2Shell operational page”, October 2026 and in CERT-EU, “Security advisory 2026-018”, October 2026.

Several GitHub repositories claim to host proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. JFrog, “PHP2Shell: all you need to know”, October 2026 reports that some are pranks, one of which changes the victim’s wallpaper. Treat every unofficial PoC as untrusted code.

Bitdefender telemetry has observed no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication, and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation. This is a time-bound observation and not evidence that the threat is overstated. Any change will be recorded in Advisory History.

A Disclosure Is Not an Exploitation

Much of the early coverage of PHP2Shell blurs two different events, and the difference changes what you should do.

A vulnerability disclosure says a flaw exists, how severe it could be, and which versions fix it. The CVSS score of 9.2 describes what an attacker could do, not what any attacker has done. A disclosure carries no evidence that anyone is attacking anything.

A proof of concept is code that demonstrates the flaw. Proofs of concept range from working research tools to broken or malicious fakes, as the repositories above show. A working proof of concept lowers the cost of an attack but is not an attack.

Exploitation in the wild means someone has used the flaw against real systems that did not belong to them, and defenders have the evidence: requests, crashes, shells, files. Only this stage justifies statements such as “customers are being compromised.”

PHP2Shell sits between the second and third stages. It is disclosed and patched. Working proofs of concept exist in researchers’ hands, and Calif’s video showed one against a number of targets. PHP’s team saw no functional exploits at release. Datadog attributes exploitation attempts to AWS from 2026-10-17, which we have not confirmed, and Bitdefender telemetry shows none. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are watching for the next step.

Two conclusions follow, and they point the same direction. Do not treat the absence of confirmed attacks as a reason to wait, because the flaw needs no login and no application bug, and the proofs of concept and fixed code are public. And do not treat the severity score as proof of compromise: patch first, then check for compromise using the signals in What To Do, instead of assuming the worst.

How It Can Be Exploited

PHP runs behind the web server through a SAPI (Server API), the interface that hands each request to PHP. The two most common are mod_php, where PHP is loaded directly into the Apache web server’s own processes, and PHP-FPM, a separate pool of PHP worker processes that the web server forwards requests to. Both CVEs are memory corruption bugs, meaning the attacker causes PHP to read or write memory it should not, inside those worker processes.

On mod_php, exploitation happens during request initialization, before any application code runs. We assess that PHP2Shell is a runtime bug, not an application bug: on mod_php, CMS updates, plugin hygiene and application hardening do not change exposure. The attacker needs no login and no flaw in WordPress, Drupal or the custom code behind the site.

We assess with high confidence that exploitation attempts will follow. Calif’s video of a working proof of concept, Wiz’s demonstrations against common CMS container images, and Wiz’s report that frontier AI models lowered the cost of building exploits all shorten the path from disclosure to attack. The attack follows the established pattern for internet-facing remote code execution: scanning first, though version fingerprinting is unreliable here, then initial access through one of two paths. CVE-2026-109618 uses a single oversized request to corrupt memory while PHP is still setting the request up. CVE-2026-109619 reuses memory left behind by an earlier request on the same worker. No public source yet documents the automated phase, the hand-off to human operators, or post-exploitation activity for PHP2Shell specifically. The established pattern for comparable flaws is a first shell, a reverse shell back to attacker infrastructure, a webshell for persistent access, tool downloads, privilege escalation and persistence. These are the stages defenders should prepare for, not observed PHP2Shell behavior.

Exposure requires an unpatched PHP branch serving web requests. The demonstrated application-independent path is mod_php. CVE-2026-109619 additionally needs session.upload_progress.enabled left at its default of on, and attacker requests landing on the same worker, while its fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only. Several things limit how many attempts succeed: CVE-2026-109618 also requires defeating ASLR (address space layout randomization, which places code at unpredictable memory addresses), the same-worker requirement constrains CVE-2026-109619, and public PoCs are unreliable. Other factors widen the blast radius: no authentication, no application flaw needed on mod_php, and a default-on setting in the CVE-2026-109619 path. Wiz reports versions back to PHP 5.4 are affected, and branches 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have no official fix. The version string is unreliable in both directions: distribution backports fix the bug without changing the version, so scanners flag patched hosts, while “latest available” on an end-of-life branch still means vulnerable. Exploitation attempts are reported by a named third party and are expected; successful exploitation at scale is not established.

Hunting guidance from other vendors, including Datadog, points defenders at crash evidence: memory exhaustion errors at initialization and Apache segmentation faults. A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running. Crash logs measure attempts, not compromises.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How It Works

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption). An out-of-memory condition (PHP running out of its allowed memory) interrupts PHP while request data is only partly initialized, and the cleanup routine then treats the half-built data as valid. Datadog describes the trigger as an unauthenticated POST request with a single very long form field name, about 3.5 MB in the lab. When the attempt crashes or fails, PHP logs a memory exhaustion error reported as “Unknown on line 0”.

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state). Request-owned state survives after its memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker reuses it. This is a use-after-free: the program keeps using a pointer to memory it has already released, which an attacker can refill with data they control. The path requires session.upload_progress.enabled, the setting that tracks file upload progress in the user’s session and is on by default. The fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only.

On Apache, a crashed worker appears in the error log as AH00052, the message Apache writes when a child process exits on a signal such as a segmentation fault. A successful exploit can avoid both this entry and the memory exhaustion error.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

Read the PHP version and the Server API line from a phpinfo page served by the web server: a one-line file containing <?php phpinfo(); placed temporarily in the web root, which prints the running build’s configuration. Delete it immediately afterward, because it exposes that configuration to anyone who requests it. Do not rely on php -v, which reports the command-line binary and not necessarily the build the web server runs. On Apache, apachectl -M | grep -i php lists a loaded PHP module if mod_php is in use; systemctl list-units | grep php shows running php-fpm services. For distribution packages, search the package changelog for the CVE IDs, because a backported fix may not change the version number: on RHEL-family systems, rpm -q --changelog php-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]'; on Debian or Ubuntu, apt changelog php8.x-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]', substituting your branch for 8.x. For containers, check base image tags, especially WordPress, Drupal and Joomla images.

SAPI

Exploitability

mod_php

Application-independent RCE demonstrated

PHP-FPM

Susceptible; see the open PHP-FPM note in How it Works

php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed

In scope per PHP; no public exploitability analysis

2. Patch or Mitigate

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Branches 7.4, 8.0, 8.1 and older have no official fix; moving to a supported branch is the only reliable answer, and unofficial backports are unvetted. PHP states: “there are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice.” Where patching must wait:

Mitigation (all partial)

Addresses

session.upload_progress.enabled=0; on PHP 8.5 also fatal_error_backtraces=0

CVE-2026-109619

pm.max_requests=1 on PHP-FPM (each worker exits after one request, breaking the same-worker requirement; costs a process start per request)

CVE-2026-109619 on FPM

memory_limit=-1 combined with request-size limits at the web server or proxy and container memory limits; do not use the operating system’s per-process limits (RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_DATA) for this

CVE-2026-109618

WAF or reverse-proxy blocking

Both, partial

Restart all PHP workers after any configuration change; running workers keep the old settings.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

A clean error log does not clear a host. Look for:

Very large requests in proxy or WAF logs, consistent with a multi-megabyte form field name. Request bodies are often not logged, so look at request size. This applies to CVE-2026-109618 only; no log signature has been published for CVE-2026-109619.

“Unknown on line 0” memory exhaustion errors and AH00052 entries (failed or crashed attempts).

Shell processes whose parent is a web worker (apache2, httpd, php-fpm, php-cgi).

New script files in upload, cache and tmp directories.

Start the lookback at 2026-10-17, the earliest attempts reported by Datadog. If you find a compromise, rotate the secrets the PHP process could read: application database credentials, API keys in environment variables or configuration files, and cloud credentials present on the host.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Watch this advisory, the PHP advisory and CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog for updates. Keep alerting on child processes of web workers, and keep software inventory current in GravityZone so hunting can be scoped to hosts running PHP.

Indicators of Compromise

Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication and we have no indicators of compromise to share.

GravityZone Coverage

The PHP2Shell exploit is memory corruption inside the PHP worker, so GravityZone detection focuses on what the attacker does with the access it gives: starting a shell, opening a reverse shell, planting a webshell, downloading tools, escalating privileges and persisting. These actions are where the attack becomes visible, and where the detections below fire.

Bitdefender MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring and active response, and the MDR team is actively hunting for PHP2Shell together with Bitdefender Labs. MDR uses software inventory to scope hunts to systems running PHP, so keeping inventory current in GravityZone helps.

External Attack Surface Management (EASM) applies because the vulnerable PHP service is internet-facing: it identifies exposed assets from outside the perimeter without an agent, unlike Risk Management, which scans managed endpoints. EASM detects the PHP version on exposed assets, so it can show which of your internet-facing services run an affected version.

GravityZone Risk Management detects the PHP version installed on managed endpoints and compares it with data from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and the security advisories of specific Linux distributions (Ubuntu, CentOS and Red Hat). It flags vulnerable versions and the CVEs that apply to them.

The rules below come from Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), Advanced Threat Control (ATC), and Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction (PHASR). Rules marked blocking stop the post-exploitation action, not the exploit.

Linux

Three detections work; however, PHP is deployed (Apache module, PHP-FPM or php-cgi):

First shell: Anomaly.Process.NewProcessStartedShell

Reverse shell: EDR.PhpReverseShell, ATC.BashReverseShell.X (blocking)

The rest of the Linux detections are tied to the web worker process and fire for Apache mod_php and php-cgi, not when the parent process is PHP-FPM:

First shell: EDR.WebServiceSpawnShell

Reverse shell: EDR.WebReverseShell (incident), the generic reverse-shell rule family

Hands-on activity: EDR.SuspiciousWebServerBehaviour and .2, EDR.Generic.Nexus.WebServer

Webshell: EDR.WebServiceWriteScript

Windows

On Windows, PHP typically runs as php-cgi.exe, and alerts such as SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell already monitor php-cgi and other web server configurations. ATC has heuristics that detect command shells started by php-cgi.exe when post-exploitation actions follow through those shells, such as enumeration, credential dumping or adding a new user to the machine. Because both flaws require heap manipulation (the attacker shaping how PHP lays out memory), Process Introspection also detects suspicious process creation from memory pages that do not belong to a loaded module. Process Introspection checks the state of a process during key operations such as creating a child process, which is where an exploited PHP worker would start a shell.

Hands-on recon: SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell (104852)

Webshell: SuspiciousServerRootFile (100942), WebShellCreation (102198)

Reverse shell: PossibleReverseShellSocketPipeChild and Parent (103945, 103946), PythonReverseShell (102194), the NetCat rules, Empire.Stager.WAR (105626)

Tool download: CertutilDownload, PotentialIngressToolTransferViaCURL

Persistence: NewScheduledTask, PowershellScheduledTaskCreated

PHASR (blocking): whoami, certutil, curl and PowerShell downloads, account creation, local admin group changes, schtasks

macOS (PHP under Apache httpd or php-fpm)

First shell: EDR.WebService.ShellSpawned

Reverse shell: EDR.Metasploit.PhpMeterpreter, EDR.Metasploit.ReversePhpSsl.N and Payload.ReversePhpSSL.Y, ATC.Metasploit.Payload.ReversePhpSSL.X (blocks on execution), the reverse-shell rule family, PHASR Bash reverse shell and Netcat (blocking)

Tool download: Anomaly.Process.DownloaderNewArguments, PHASR Curl (blocking)

Hands-on activity: Anomaly.Process.NewSubprocessesStarted, EDR.HiddenFileExecution

Persistence: EDR.SuspiciousCrontabModification, PHASR.Crontab.InstallOtherUser (blocking)

View CSAF

Summary

Multiple SIMATIC WinCC versions are affected by a database privilege escalation vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user with access to the database to execute commands on the underlying host system. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens WinCC are affected:

SIMATIC WinCC V7.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-59241)

SIMATIC WinCC V8.0 vers:intdot/<8.0.0.11 (CVE-2026-59241)

SIMATIC WinCC V8.1 vers:intdot/<8.1.7 (CVE-2026-59241)

CVSS

Vendor

Equipment

CVSS v3 8.8

Vendor Siemens

Equipment SIMATIC WinCC V7.5

1 Vulnerability

1 Vulnerability Incorrect Privilege Assignment

Background

Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-59241

The affected application does not sufficiently restrict the permissions assigned to a database role. This could allow an authenticated remote attacker with database access to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary commands on the host system where SIMATIC WinCC is installed, potentially leading to a compromise of the system.
